## 1. Definition and epidemiology
- **Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH):** spectrum from **acetabular dysplasia** (shallow acetabulum) through **subluxation** to **frank dislocation** (dislocatable or dislocated), developing **before or after birth** (hence "developmental", not "congenital").
- **Incidence:** **instability about 1-2 per 100 newborns at birth** (most resolve), **true dislocation about 1-1.5 per 1,000**.
- **Teratologic dislocation** (separate entity): dislocated **in utero**, **irreducible**, with **neuromuscular syndromes** (**arthrogryposis, myelomeningocele, Larsen syndrome**): worse prognosis, early open reduction.

## 2. Risk factors ("4 Fs" + others)
- **Female (about 4-6:1; maternal relaxin sensitivity)**, **First-born** (tight uterus), **Family history (about 10-12x risk with an affected sibling or parent)**, **breech presentation ("Frank breech": hips flexed, knees extended: strongest single risk factor)**.
- **Oligohydramnios**, **left hip (about 60%; left occiput anterior position against the maternal sacrum)**, bilateral in about 20%.
- **"Packaging" disorders** (associated conditions from intrauterine crowding): **congenital muscular torticollis**, **metatarsus adductus**, **congenital knee dislocation**, **calcaneovalgus/clubfoot** (association weaker).
- **Postnatal swaddling with hips extended and adducted** (Native American, Japanese cultural practices; **"hip-healthy swaddling" with hips free to flex and abduct**).
- **Ethnicity:** higher in Native Americans and Sami; low in Africans (carrying on the back with hips abducted).

## 3. Pathoanatomy
- **Obstacles to reduction (acetabular side, in order):**
  - **Intra-articular:** **inverted/hypertrophied labrum ("limbus")**, **hypertrophied ligamentum teres**, **pulvinar (fibrofatty tissue in the acetabular floor)**, **contracted inferior capsule**, **transverse acetabular ligament** (hypertrophied).
  - **Extra-articular:** **iliopsoas tendon** (creates an **hourglass constriction of the capsule**), **adductor longus** (contracture).
- **Secondary changes:** **shallow, anteverted acetabulum**, **increased femoral anteversion**, **coxa valga**, **false acetabulum (in neglected cases)**, **neolimbus** formation.

## 4. Clinical examination by age
### Newborn (up to about 3 months)
- **Barlow test** (**adduction + posterior pressure on the flexed hip: dislocatable hip**: **"Barlow = Bye-bye"**).
- **Ortolani test** (**abduction + elevation of the greater trochanter: reduces a dislocated hip with a "clunk"**: **"Ortolani = Out to In"**).
- **High-pitched clicks** (soft tissue) are not significant.
- **Both tests become negative after about 3 months** as soft tissues tighten (dislocated hips become irreducible and fixed).
### Older infant (over 3 months)
- **Limited abduction (most reliable sign: under 60 degrees in flexion or asymmetry)**.
- **Galeazzi (Allis) sign**: **apparent femoral shortening** with hips and knees flexed (unilateral dislocation; **negative in bilateral DDH**).
- **Asymmetric thigh/gluteal skin folds** (unreliable), **Klisic test** (line from the ASIS through the greater trochanter passes below the umbilicus in a dislocated hip).
### Walking child
- **Trendelenburg gait**, **limp**, **leg-length discrepancy**, **waddling gait** (bilateral), **hyperlordosis** (bilateral).

## 5. Imaging
### Ultrasound (up to about 4-6 months: before the femoral head ossific nucleus appears)
- **Graf method (static, coronal view):**
  - **Alpha angle** (**bony roof**: angle between the baseline (ilium) and the bony acetabular roof line): **normal 60 degrees or more**.
  - **Beta angle** (**cartilaginous roof**: baseline to the labrum/cartilage roof line): **normal under 55 degrees** (increases as the head displaces).
| Graf type | Alpha | Beta | Description | Management |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **I** | **≥60** | <55 | **Normal (mature)** | None |
| **IIa** | 50-59 | 55-77 | **Physiological immaturity (under 3 months)** | **Repeat ultrasound at 6 weeks to 3 months** |
| **IIb** | 50-59 | | Delayed ossification (**over 3 months**) | **Pavlik harness** |
| **IIc** | **43-49** | <77 | **Critical** (stable or unstable) | **Pavlik** |
| **D** | 43-49 | **>77** | **Decentring** (about to dislocate) | **Pavlik** |
| **III** | **<43** | >77 | **Dislocated (cartilage roof pushed up)** | Pavlik/closed reduction |
| **IV** | <43 | Labrum inverted (pushed down) | **Dislocated (labrum inverted)** | Closed/open reduction |
- **Dynamic ultrasound (Harcke)**: stability; **femoral head coverage (Terjesen/Morin): under 50% abnormal**.
- **Selective ultrasound screening** (**UK NIPE**: risk factors (**breech at or after 36 weeks, family history**) or abnormal examination: **ultrasound by 6 weeks**) vs **universal ultrasound screening** (Austria, Germany: more treatment, possibly fewer late cases).
### Radiographs (after about 4-6 months, once the ossific nucleus appears)
- **Hilgenreiner line** (horizontal through the triradiate cartilages), **Perkin line** (vertical from the lateral acetabular margin): **normal: femoral head ossific nucleus (or medial metaphyseal beak) in the inferomedial quadrant**.
- **Shenton line** (broken in subluxation/dislocation).
- **Acetabular index** (**normal under about 30 degrees at birth, decreasing to under 20-25 degrees by 2 years**): increased in dysplasia.
- **Delayed appearance of the ossific nucleus** on the affected side.
- **Centre-edge angle of Wiberg (after about 5 years): normal over 20-25 degrees**.
- **Arthrography** (at the time of closed reduction): **medial dye pool (under 5 mm = acceptable concentric reduction)**, inverted limbus, **"rose thorn" sign** (normal labrum).
- **MRI/CT after reduction** in spica: confirm reduction (**MRI preferred: no radiation**).

## 6. Treatment by age
### 0-6 months: Pavlik harness
- **Dynamic flexion-abduction orthosis**: **hips flexed about 100 degrees** (anterior straps), **abduction by gravity in the "safe zone" (Ramsey)** (posterior straps loose: prevent adduction but do not force abduction).
- **Safe zone (Ramsey):** the arc between **maximum abduction** and the **position of redislocation (adduction)**: **avoid forced abduction over about 60 degrees** (**AVN**).
- **Positioning errors:**
  - **Excessive flexion (over 120 degrees)**: **femoral nerve palsy** (commonest nerve complication; quadriceps weakness: **stop/adjust harness**), **inferior (obturator) dislocation**,
  - **Insufficient flexion**: failure to reduce,
  - **Forced abduction**: **AVN of the femoral head**,
  - **Brachial plexus palsy** (shoulder straps too tight), skin breakdown.
- **Monitor with ultrasound**: **if not reduced by 3-4 weeks, abandon the Pavlik** (**"Pavlik harness disease"**: **erosion of the posterior acetabular wall** from prolonged use with a persistently dislocated (posterior) head).
- **Success:** **about 90%+ for dysplastic/subluxated hips**, **about 80-85% for dislocated (Ortolani-positive) hips**; **less effective with Graf IV, bilateral dislocations, Barlow-negative irreducible hips, older age (over 7 weeks at initiation), absent Ortolani sign**.
- **Duration:** full-time until stable (usually about **6-12 weeks**) then weaning.
### 6-18 months: closed reduction + hip spica
- **Under general anaesthesia**, **arthrogram**, **percutaneous adductor tenotomy** (increases the safe zone).
- **Hip spica cast in "human position" (Salter): hip flexion about 100 degrees, abduction about 40-50 degrees (avoid over 60), neutral rotation**: **about 3 months** in spica (change at 6 weeks), then abduction brace.
- **Post-reduction imaging: MRI or CT** (concentricity).
- **Traction before reduction** (historical: to reduce AVN): **not supported by evidence**.
- **Ossific nucleus presence:** does not affect AVN risk significantly in most studies; **delaying reduction until it appears is not recommended**.
### Open reduction: indications
- **Failed closed reduction** (**medial dye pool over 5-7 mm**, unstable in the safe zone, **excessive abduction needed**), **age over about 18-24 months** (variable), **teratologic** dislocation.
- **Approaches:**
  - **Medial approach (Ludloff: between adductor brevis and pectineus/iliopsoas; or Ferguson: posterior to adductor brevis)**: **under about 12-18 months**; addresses medial obstacles (**iliopsoas, ligamentum teres, transverse acetabular ligament, inferior capsule**); **cannot perform capsulorrhaphy**; **medial femoral circumflex artery at risk: higher AVN**.
  - **Anterior (anterolateral, Smith-Petersen/bikini) approach**: **over about 12-18 months**; allows **capsulorrhaphy** and **concomitant pelvic osteotomy**; **iliopsoas tenotomy**, **inverted labrum**, pulvinar.
### Over 18-24 months to 8 years: open reduction + femoral and/or pelvic osteotomy
- **Femoral shortening osteotomy** (**reduces pressure on the head: lowers AVN and redislocation**) + **varus derotation** if needed.
- **Pelvic osteotomies:**
  - **Redirectional (reshaping the acetabulum: requires a concentrically reduced, congruous hip)**:
    - **Salter innominate osteotomy** (**single cut above the acetabulum from the sciatic notch to the AIIS; hinges on the pubic symphysis**: **anterolateral coverage**; **age 18 months to about 6 years**; **acetabular index correction up to about 10-15 degrees**; open triradiate cartilage),
    - **Triple innominate osteotomy (Steel, Tönnis)** (**older children/adolescents**; ilium, ischium, pubis),
    - **Periacetabular osteotomy (Bernese/Ganz PAO)** (**closed triradiate cartilage: adolescents and adults**; **posterior column preserved**: allows early weight bearing, preserves pelvic ring),
  - **Reshaping (volume-reducing: incomplete osteotomies hinging on the triradiate cartilage; for capacious acetabula; open triradiate cartilage):**
    - **Pemberton (pericapsular)** (**hinges on the triradiate cartilage**; **reduces acetabular volume**; **anterolateral coverage**; **age 18 months to 10 years**),
    - **Dega** (hinges on the triradiate cartilage; **posterolateral coverage**: **neuromuscular dysplasia (cerebral palsy: posterosuperior deficiency)**),
    - **San Diego** (neuromuscular).
  - **Salvage (augmenting with capsular interposition: fibrocartilage metaplasia; for incongruent hips):**
    - **Chiari osteotomy** (**medial displacement of the acetabulum beneath the ilium**: **capsule interposed**),
    - **Shelf procedure (Staheli)** (bone graft extending the lateral acetabulum).
### Over 8 years (bilateral) or over about 10 years (unilateral)
- **Reduction often not attempted** for **high bilateral dislocations without a false acetabulum** (**better function than with AVN/failed reduction**); unilateral: still possible in selected cases; **salvage/arthroplasty later**.

## 7. Complications
- **Avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head**: **the most important iatrogenic complication**; caused by **forced abduction, excessive pressure, medial circumflex artery injury**: **Kalamchi and MacEwen classification**:
  - **Group I:** **changes in the ossific nucleus only** (best prognosis),
  - **Group II:** **lateral physeal damage** (**valgus tilt** of the head, **lateral growth arrest**),
  - **Group III:** **central physeal damage** (short neck, **coxa breva**, trochanteric overgrowth),
  - **Group IV:** **total head and physeal damage** (worst).
  - (**Bucholz-Ogden classification** also used.)
- **Redislocation**, **residual dysplasia** (needs pelvic osteotomy), **femoral nerve palsy** (Pavlik), **Pavlik disease**, **stiffness**, **early OA** (**the commonest long-term sequela: the leading cause of THA under age 40-50**), **leg-length discrepancy**, **trochanteric overgrowth** (**greater trochanteric epiphysiodesis or advancement**).
- **Residual dysplasia** is followed with serial radiographs to skeletal maturity.

## 8. Adult sequelae (DDH in adults)
- **Crowe classification (proximal migration of the femoral head)**: **I under 50% subluxation**, **II 50-75%**, **III 75-100%**, **IV over 100% (high dislocation)**.
- **Hartofilakidis:** **dysplasia**, **low dislocation** (false acetabulum overlapping the true), **high dislocation** (no contact).
- **THA in DDH:** **cup in the true acetabulum** (low hip centre), **small cups**, **structural autograft (femoral head) for superolateral deficiency**, **subtrochanteric shortening osteotomy (Crowe IV)** (lengthening **over about 4 cm: sciatic nerve palsy risk**), **excessive femoral anteversion (modular/cemented stems)**.

> Exam pearl: **Barlow = dislocatable (adduct + push back); Ortolani = dislocated reduces (abduct + lift). After 3 months: limited abduction is the best sign; Galeazzi negative if bilateral. Breech + female + first-born + family history.**

> Exam pearl: **Graf: alpha ≥60 = type I; IIa physiological under 3 months; under 43 = dislocated (III/IV). Ultrasound under 4-6 months, radiographs after (Hilgenreiner, Perkin, Shenton, acetabular index).**

> Exam pearl: **0-6 months Pavlik (flexion about 100, no forced abduction; excess flexion = femoral nerve palsy; stop at 3-4 weeks if not reduced: Pavlik disease). 6-18 months closed reduction + spica (human position, adductor tenotomy, medial dye pool under 5 mm). Over 18-24 months open reduction + femoral shortening ± pelvic osteotomy. AVN (Kalamchi-MacEwen) from forced abduction.**

> Exam pearl: **Salter: hinge at symphysis, open triradiate, congruent hip. Pemberton/Dega: hinge at the triradiate (Dega: CP, posterior coverage). PAO: closed triradiate, posterior column intact. Chiari/shelf: salvage for incongruent hips (capsular metaplasia).**

# Part A: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (LCPD)

## 1. Definition and epidemiology
- **Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis in a child**, followed by **fragmentation, revascularisation and remodelling** (self-limiting but may leave a deformed head).
- **Age 4-8 years (range 2-12)**; **boys about 4-5:1**; **bilateral in about 10-15%** (**asynchronous**: **symmetric simultaneous bilateral involvement suggests an alternative diagnosis: multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (MED), hypothyroidism, sickle cell, Gaucher, spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia**).
- **Associations:** **delayed bone age (about 90%)**, **short stature**, **low birth weight**, **ADHD/hyperactivity**, **passive smoking**, **low socioeconomic status**, **thrombophilia (protein C/S deficiency, factor V Leiden: controversial)**, **inguinal hernia**, genitourinary anomalies.

## 2. Pathogenesis
- **Single or repeated interruption of the blood supply** (**lateral epiphyseal vessels from the medial femoral circumflex artery**) to the capital femoral epiphysis (**at age 4-7, the epiphysis depends almost entirely on the lateral epiphyseal vessels**: the **ligamentum teres artery contributes little** and the **metaphyseal vessels do not cross the physis**).
- **Stages (Waldenström):**
  1. **Initial (sclerosis/necrosis)**: **sclerotic, smaller ossific nucleus**, **widened medial joint space**, **subchondral fracture ("crescent sign": Caffey sign)**: about 6 months,
  2. **Fragmentation (resorption)**: **fragmented epiphysis**, lateral extrusion, **most mechanically vulnerable stage** (deformation): about 1 year,
  3. **Reossification (healing)**: new bone formation: about 3-5 years,
  4. **Residual (healed)**: final shape (**coxa magna, coxa plana, short neck, trochanteric overgrowth**).

## 3. Clinical features
- **Painless (or mild) limp** (**commonest presentation**), **pain referred to the knee/thigh** (obturator nerve), **antalgic or Trendelenburg gait**, **limited abduction and internal rotation** (most important; **loss of abduction = poor prognosis**), thigh atrophy, mild shortening.
- **Differential diagnosis:** **transient synovitis**, **septic arthritis**, **MED/SED**, **hypothyroidism**, **sickle cell disease**, **Gaucher disease**, **steroid-induced AVN**, **Meyer dysplasia** (**irregular ossification of the femoral head under 4 years**, often bilateral: **self-resolving**).

## 4. Imaging
- **Radiographs (AP and frog-leg lateral)**: stages, **crescent sign (subchondral fracture: earliest radiographic sign)**, head-at-risk signs.
- **MRI** (early diagnosis, extent of necrosis, **perfusion MRI**), **bone scan** (avascularity; early).
- **Arthrography** (dynamic: **hinge abduction**, containability).

## 5. Classifications
### Herring lateral pillar classification (**most widely used; prognosis; assessed at the start of the fragmentation stage**)
- **Lateral pillar** = lateral 15-30% of the epiphysis on AP radiograph.
| Group | Lateral pillar height | Prognosis |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | **Intact (100%)** | **Good regardless of age** |
| **B** | **Over 50% maintained** | Good if **under 8 years at onset** (bone age under 6) |
| **B/C border** | **About 50%**, narrow (2-3 mm) or poorly ossified pillar, or exactly 50% | Intermediate |
| **C** | **Under 50% maintained** | **Poor** (regardless of treatment, especially older) |
### Catterall classification (extent of head involvement: I-IV; **interobserver reliability poor**)
- **I: anterior head only (under 25%)**; **II: under 50% (anterior + central sequestrum)**; **III: over 50% (only medial/posterior spared)**; **IV: whole head**.
- **Catterall "head-at-risk" signs (poor prognosis):**
  1. **Gage sign** (V-shaped radiolucency in the lateral epiphysis/metaphysis),
  2. **Calcification lateral to the epiphysis** (lateral extrusion),
  3. **Lateral subluxation of the femoral head**,
  4. **Horizontal growth plate**,
  5. **Metaphyseal cysts (diffuse metaphyseal reaction)**.
### Salter-Thompson classification
- **A: subchondral fracture under 50% of the head; B: over 50%** (prognostic; in the early stage).
### Stulberg classification (outcome at maturity: **predicts OA risk**)
| Class | Head shape | Congruency | OA risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| **I** | **Normal (spherical)** | **Spherical congruency** | **None** |
| **II** | **Spherical but larger (coxa magna), short neck or steep acetabulum** | **Spherical congruency** | Minimal |
| **III** | **Ovoid/mushroom-shaped (not flat)** | **Aspherical congruency** | **Mild-moderate OA in later adulthood** |
| **IV** | **Flat head (over 1 cm flat weight-bearing surface) + flat acetabulum** | **Aspherical congruency** | **Moderate OA (in middle age)** |
| **V** | **Flat head with normal acetabulum** | **Aspherical incongruency** | **Severe early OA** |

## 6. Prognostic factors
- **Age at onset (most important): under 6 years: good prognosis** (more remodelling time); **over 8 years: poor**.
- **Lateral pillar classification (Herring)** (most important radiographic predictor), **extent of head involvement**, **head-at-risk signs**, **female sex** (worse: earlier skeletal maturity), **loss of hip motion (abduction)**, **hinge abduction**, **Stulberg class at maturity**.

## 7. Management (principle: containment)
- **Goals:** **maintain the femoral head within the acetabulum (containment)** during the vulnerable fragmentation stage, so that the acetabulum acts as a mould; **maintain ROM** (especially **abduction**).
- **Non-operative:**
  - **Under 6 years (bone age), all groups (mostly):** **observation, activity modification, physiotherapy (ROM, abduction stretching)**, NSAIDs for synovitis; **bracing (Petrie casts/abduction orthoses)**: largely abandoned (no proven benefit).
- **Operative containment (Herring prospective study: 2004):**
  - **Over 8 years (chronological; bone age over 6) with lateral pillar B or B/C**: **surgical containment (proximal femoral varus osteotomy or Salter innominate osteotomy) gives better results than non-operative treatment**.
  - **Group A**: good outcome regardless.
  - **Group C**: poor outcome regardless of treatment (in most series).
  - **Under 8 years with B**: good outcomes without surgery.
- **Containment procedures:**
  - **Proximal femoral varus (derotation) osteotomy (VDRO)**: **about 15-20 degrees varus**; **shortening, Trendelenburg gait (abductor weakness), trochanteric overgrowth** (often remodels in young children),
  - **Salter innominate osteotomy** (**anterolateral coverage**; lengthens slightly; **requires near-full abduction**),
  - **Shelf acetabuloplasty**, **triple innominate osteotomy**, **combined femoral and pelvic osteotomies** for severe cases.
- **Hinge abduction (salvage: non-containable head; the extruded head hinges on the lateral acetabular edge in abduction):**
  - **Valgus (extension) osteotomy** (**brings the congruent part of the head into the weight-bearing zone; improves adduction-abduction mechanics**), **Chiari osteotomy**, **shelf procedure**, **cheilectomy** (removing the lateral prominence: risk of AVN/physeal injury).
- **Late sequelae:**
  - **Trochanteric overgrowth (relative)**: **greater trochanteric epiphysiodesis (under 8 years)** or **trochanteric advancement (Wagner)**.
  - **FAI (cam-type from a mushroom head)**: **surgical hip dislocation with femoral head reduction osteotomy**, **relative femoral neck lengthening**, osteochondroplasty.
  - **Osteochondritis dissecans of the femoral head**, **labral tears**, **OA (THA in adulthood)**.

# Part B: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE)

## 8. Definition and epidemiology
- **Displacement of the proximal femoral metaphysis anteriorly and superiorly (externally rotated) relative to the epiphysis** (the **epiphysis stays in the acetabulum** and is **posterior and inferior** relative to the neck) through the **hypertrophic zone of the physis**.
- **Commonest adolescent hip disorder**: **age 10-16 (boys: about 13-14; girls: about 11-12)**, **boys more than girls (about 1.5-2:1)**, **left more than right**, **bilateral in about 20-40% (up to 60% eventually; about 20% at presentation)**.
- **Obesity (strongest association: over 95th percentile BMI in about 50-80%)**, **African-American and Polynesian ethnicity**.
- **Endocrine/metabolic causes (atypical SCFE: suspect if under 10 years or over 16, below 50th percentile weight, short stature):** **hypothyroidism (commonest endocrine)**, **growth hormone deficiency/supplementation**, **renal osteodystrophy (chronic renal failure)**, **hypogonadism**, **panhypopituitarism**, **radiotherapy**, **Down syndrome**. **Bilateral slips are much more common in endocrine SCFE** (**prophylactic pinning recommended**).
- **Biomechanics:** **increased shear forces** (obesity, **femoral retroversion**, **physeal obliquity: more vertical physis in adolescence**), **perichondrial ring thinning** during growth spurt, **hormonal (oestrogen protects; testosterone weakens the physis)**.

## 9. Classification
### Loder (stability; prognostic: **the most important**)
- **Stable: able to bear weight (with or without crutches)**: **AVN risk about 0-5%**.
- **Unstable: unable to bear weight (even with crutches)**: **AVN risk about 20-50%** (Loder: 47%).
### Temporal (traditional)
- **Acute (symptoms under 3 weeks)**, **chronic (over 3 weeks: commonest; remodelling of the metaphysis, posteroinferior callus)**, **acute-on-chronic**.
### Southwick slip angle (severity; on frog-leg lateral)
- **Epiphyseal-shaft angle difference vs the contralateral normal side:** **mild under 30 degrees**, **moderate 30-50 degrees**, **severe over 50 degrees**.
### Wilson (displacement on AP)
- **Mild under 33%**, **moderate 33-50%**, **severe over 50%** of the metaphyseal width.

## 10. Clinical features
- **Groin, thigh or KNEE pain** (**obturator nerve referred pain: knee pain in an adolescent = examine the hip**: **delayed diagnosis common**), **limp**, **out-toeing**.
- **Obligatory external rotation with hip flexion (Drehmann sign)**, **loss of internal rotation** (most sensitive), loss of abduction and flexion, **shortening**.
- **Unstable:** acute severe pain, **unable to bear weight**, limb externally rotated and shortened (like a femoral neck fracture).

## 11. Imaging
- **AP and frog-leg lateral pelvis** (**frog-leg lateral avoided in unstable slips**: **cross-table lateral instead**: may displace further).
- **Signs:**
  - **Klein line** (**line along the superior femoral neck on AP should intersect the lateral epiphysis; in SCFE it does not or intersects less than the normal side**: **Trethowan sign**),
  - **Widened, irregular physis** (early pre-slip),
  - **Metaphyseal blanch sign of Steel** (**double density: overlap of the displaced epiphysis on the metaphysis**),
  - **Reduced epiphyseal height**,
  - **Capener sign** (loss of the normal triangular overlap of the medial metaphysis with the posterior acetabular wall).
- **MRI:** **pre-slip (physeal widening, marrow oedema)**; the contralateral hip; AVN.
- **Bone age:** Oxford, **triradiate cartilage open = higher contralateral slip risk**; **Risser**; **modified Oxford score**.

## 12. Management
### Stable SCFE
- **Urgent (not emergency) admission, non-weight bearing**, then **in situ fixation with a single cannulated screw** (**"pin in situ": do NOT attempt reduction: AVN risk**):
  - **Screw perpendicular to the physis, in the centre of the epiphysis on both views**, entering **anterior on the femoral neck** (because the epiphysis is posterior: **anterior-to-posterior trajectory**),
  - **At least 5 threads (about 4-5 threads) across the physis**; **tip at least 5 mm from the subchondral bone** (**avoid joint penetration: chondrolysis**: **"approach-withdraw" technique** and multiple fluoroscopic views to exclude penetration),
  - **Single central screw for stable slips** (**two screws for unstable slips** add rotational stability but increase penetration risk).
- **Physeal closure** after fixation usually within about 1 year.
### Unstable SCFE
- **Emergency (controversial timing): gentle positional/incidental reduction**, **capsular decompression (arthrotomy/aspiration: reduces intracapsular tamponade)**, **fixation with one or two screws**; **urgent fixation within 24 hours** (some evidence for lower AVN); **avoid forceful manipulation**.
- **Modified Dunn procedure (subcapital realignment via surgical hip dislocation: Ganz approach)**: **anatomic reduction with preservation of the retinacular vessels** (**extended retinacular flap**); for **unstable and severe stable slips** in experienced centres; **AVN about 0-25% (debated)**; **intraoperative monitoring of head perfusion (drill hole bleeding, ICP monitoring)**.
### Severe chronic/stable slips with deformity
- **In situ pinning followed by corrective osteotomy for symptomatic FAI/deformity later:**
  - **Subcapital (cuneiform: Fish/Dunn)** (**closest to the deformity: best correction, highest AVN**),
  - **Base of neck (Kramer, Barmada)** (intermediate),
  - **Intertrochanteric (Imhäuser, Southwick: flexion-valgus-internal rotation osteotomy)** (**safest for the blood supply, compensatory, less correction**),
  - **Arthroscopic/open osteochondroplasty** for cam deformity.
### Prophylactic pinning of the contralateral hip
- **Recommended for:** **endocrine/renal SCFE**, **age under 10 years**, **open triradiate cartilage**, **poor follow-up compliance**, **modified Oxford bone age score under 16-19**, **posterior sloping angle (PSA) over about 12-14 degrees** (**increased risk of contralateral slip**). Otherwise: close follow-up.

## 13. Complications
- **AVN** (**unstable slips (up to about 50%)**, **forceful reduction**, **superior/posterosuperior screw placement** (lateral epiphyseal vessels), **subcapital osteotomy**): **the most serious complication**.
- **Chondrolysis** (**acute cartilage necrosis: joint space narrowing to under 3 mm**, painful stiffness): **unrecognised screw penetration (commonest cause)**, spica casting, **African-American/female**; **ROM physio, NSAIDs**; may need arthrodesis/THA.
- **Slip progression** (fixation failure), **contralateral slip**, **FAI (cam; pistol grip)**, **OA**, **leg-length discrepancy**, **subtrochanteric fracture** (**entry at or below the lesser trochanter** with multiple drill holes: stress riser), infection.

> Exam pearl: **Perthes: 4-8-year-old boys, delayed bone age, painless limp, loss of abduction/IR; bilateral symmetrical = think MED/hypothyroidism. Waldenström stages; crescent sign earliest. Herring lateral pillar (A/B/B-C/C) assessed in fragmentation; Catterall head-at-risk signs (Gage, lateral calcification, subluxation, horizontal physis, metaphyseal cysts).**

> Exam pearl: **Age at onset is the key prognostic factor (under 6 good). Over 8 years with B or B/C: surgical containment (femoral varus or Salter osteotomy). Hinge abduction: valgus osteotomy. Stulberg I-II good, III-IV moderate, V severe early OA (aspherical incongruity).**

> Exam pearl: **SCFE: obese adolescent with knee pain; Klein line, Steel blanch sign; Loder stable (AVN under 5%) vs unstable (up to 50%). Pin in situ with one central screw perpendicular to the physis, no reduction; joint penetration = chondrolysis. Atypical (under 10, thin, endocrine/renal) = bilateral: pin the other side. Imhäuser (intertrochanteric) safest osteotomy; modified Dunn for severe/unstable in expert hands.**
