# Part A: Congenital talipes equinovarus (CTEV, clubfoot)

## 1. Epidemiology and aetiology
- **About 1-2 per 1,000 live births** (higher in **Polynesians (about 7 per 1,000)**, lower in Chinese); **boys 2:1**; **bilateral in about 50%**.
- **Idiopathic (most)**: multifactorial; **genetic: PITX1-TBX4 pathway**, **family history (about 25% risk if a sibling and a parent are affected)**, **maternal smoking**, **early amniocentesis**; **oligohydramnios**.
- **Syndromic/non-idiopathic (stiffer, more recurrence)**: **arthrogryposis**, **myelomeningocele**, **diastrophic dysplasia** ("hitchhiker's thumb", **cauliflower ears**), **Larsen syndrome**, **Freeman-Sheldon**, **Möbius**, **amniotic band syndrome**, **tibial hemimelia**, **Pierre Robin**.
- **Associated:** **DDH** (examine the hips), **torticollis**.
- **Positional clubfoot** (intrauterine crowding): **flexible, fully correctable passively**: stretching only.

## 2. Pathoanatomy ("CAVE")
- **C**avus (**midfoot**: **forefoot pronated relative to the hindfoot**: **first ray plantarflexed**),
- **A**dductus (**forefoot adduction**: **medial subluxation of the navicular on the talar head**),
- **V**arus (**hindfoot**: **calcaneus inverted beneath the talus**),
- **E**quinus (**hindfoot/ankle**: **tight Achilles tendon**, plantarflexed talus).
- **Talus:** **neck medially and plantarly deviated (most deformed bone)**, small, plantarflexed; **navicular medially displaced, articulating with the medial side of the talar head (can reach the medial malleolus)**.
- **Calcaneus:** inverted and adducted, **rotated medially beneath the talus around the interosseous ligament** (**"calcaneus rotates under the talus"**).
- **Soft tissues:** **contracted posteromedial tissues** (**tibialis posterior, FHL, FDL, Achilles**, deltoid, spring ligament, **master knot of Henry**), **tight plantar fascia**; **calf atrophy (permanent, smaller foot and calf)**; **muscle fibrosis** (increased type I fibres and collagen).
- **Vascular:** **anterior tibial artery hypoplasia/absence** (about 85% in some studies): **caution with posterior tibial artery during surgery** (dorsalis pedis often absent).

## 3. Assessment
- **Pirani score** (6 signs, each 0, 0.5, 1; **max 6**):
  - **Midfoot contracture score (MFCS, max 3):** **curved lateral border**, **medial crease**, **lateral head of the talus coverage**,
  - **Hindfoot contracture score (HFCS, max 3):** **posterior crease**, **empty heel**, **rigid equinus**.
  - **HFCS over 2.5**: tenotomy likely needed.
- **Dimeglio classification** (**grades I-IV, 20-point scale**: soft-soft (benign) to stiff-stiff (very severe)).
- **Imaging:** not routinely needed (**ultrasound** occasionally); radiographs: **talocalcaneal parallelism** (**reduced Kite angle on AP: under 20 degrees** (normal 20-40 degrees); **lateral talocalcaneal angle under 25 degrees**).

## 4. Ponseti method (gold standard; about 95% initial correction)
- **Start early (ideally within the first 1-2 weeks of life)**; effective up to about 2 years (and even in older children with modifications).
- **Serial manipulation and long-leg (above-knee, knee flexed 90 degrees) plaster casts**, changed **weekly** (**about 5-7 casts**).
- **Order of correction: "CAVE"**:
  1. **Cavus first**: **supinate the forefoot (elevate the first ray)** to align the forefoot with the hindfoot (**never pronate**: pronation worsens cavus),
  2. **Adductus and varus together**: **abduct the supinated foot with counter-pressure on the lateral head of the talus** (**fulcrum = lateral talar head, NOT the calcaneocuboid joint**: Kite's error, which locks the calcaneus and prevents its correction),
  3. **Hindfoot varus corrects spontaneously** as the calcaneus abducts/rotates under the talus,
  4. **Equinus last**: **abduct to about 60-70 degrees (thigh-foot angle)** before addressing equinus.
- **Percutaneous Achilles tenotomy** (**about 80-90% need it**): when **dorsiflexion under 10-15 degrees** after abduction is achieved; under local anaesthetic; **final cast for 3 weeks** in about **60-70 degrees abduction and 15-20 degrees dorsiflexion**; tendon regenerates.
- **Errors:** **pronating the foot** (iatrogenic **rocker-bottom foot**), **thumb on the calcaneocuboid joint (Kite)**, **dorsiflexing before correcting varus/adduction** (**rocker-bottom/midfoot break**), **short-leg casts** (slip), **external rotation of the foot in the cast (lateral talar head as fulcrum required)**.
- **Bracing (foot abduction orthosis: Denis Browne bar / Steenbeek / Mitchell boots):** **affected foot about 60-70 degrees external rotation (abduction), normal foot about 30-40 degrees**, **shoulder-width bar**, **dorsiflexion bend about 10-15 degrees**; **23 hours/day for 3 months, then night and nap time until about 4-5 years**.
- **Non-compliance with bracing = the commonest cause of relapse** (**relapse about 10-30%**: up to 80% with poor compliance vs about 6% with good compliance).
- **Relapse:** **dynamic supination** (**overactive tibialis anterior: walking on the lateral border**), **recurrent equinus**, adduction.
  - **Repeat casting ± repeat tenotomy**.
  - **Tibialis anterior tendon transfer (TATT) to the lateral cuneiform (third cuneiform)** for **dynamic supination** in a **child over about 2.5-3 years with flexible deformity and an ossified lateral cuneiform**.
- **Atypical (complex) clubfoot** (**short, fat, stiff foot; deep plantar and posterior creases; short hyperextended first toe; equinus severe**): **modified Ponseti (Ponseti complex clubfoot protocol)**: **avoid excessive abduction**, **hyperflexion of the knee**, abduct only to about 40 degrees, use the index finger on the lateral talar head and both thumbs on the plantar metatarsal heads to correct cavus.

## 5. Surgical management (residual/neglected/syndromic)
- **Posteromedial release (PMR, Turco/McKay/Carroll; Cincinnati incision)**: **historical for primary treatment** (stiffness, overcorrection, scarring, **pain and arthritis in adulthood**); now for **resistant/syndromic** feet.
- **Bony procedures (older children):**
  - **Lateral column shortening (Evans calcaneocuboid fusion/Lichtblau resection)** (**4-8 years**),
  - **Medial column lengthening (cuneiform opening wedge) + cuboid closing-wedge osteotomy** (residual adductus),
  - **Calcaneal osteotomy (Dwyer lateral closing wedge)** for residual hindfoot varus,
  - **Talectomy** (**arthrogryposis, rigid recurrent clubfoot**),
  - **Triple arthrodesis** (**over about 10-12 years**: salvage),
  - **Ilizarov/gradual correction (Joshi's external stabilisation system: JESS; Indian contribution)** for neglected/recurrent clubfoot in older children.
- **Neglected clubfoot in older children/adults**: **Ponseti casting still useful** in walking children (good results even up to about 10 years); **JESS/Ilizarov**, **triple arthrodesis**.

# Part B: Other paediatric foot deformities

## 6. Metatarsus adductus
- **Commonest foot deformity in infants** (about 1 per 1,000); **forefoot adduction with a normal hindfoot (neutral/valgus) and normal ankle dorsiflexion** (no equinus: **distinguishes from clubfoot**); **"bean-shaped foot"**; associated with **DDH (about 5-10%)**.
- **Bleck classification** (heel bisector line): **normal: through the 2nd-3rd toe web**, **mild: through the 3rd toe**, **moderate: between the 3rd and 4th toes**, **severe: between the 4th and 5th toes**.
- **Flexibility** (passive correction beyond neutral) determines treatment: **flexible: observation/stretching (about 90% resolve spontaneously)**; **stiff/rigid: serial casting (best under 6-8 months)**; **surgery rarely** (**over 4-5 years** with persistent rigid deformity: **medial cuneiform opening wedge + cuboid closing wedge osteotomy**). **Avoid tarsometatarsal capsulotomy (Heyman-Herndon: high failure, arthritis)**.
- **Skewfoot (serpentine/Z-foot):** **forefoot adduction + hindfoot valgus** (**talonavicular lateral subluxation**): often **iatrogenic** (overcorrection of metatarsus adductus/clubfoot by casting in valgus); **medial cuneiform opening wedge + calcaneal lengthening** if symptomatic.

## 7. Congenital vertical talus (CVT; "rocker-bottom foot")
- **Irreducible dorsal dislocation of the navicular on the talar neck**, **talus vertical (plantarflexed)**, **hindfoot equinus and valgus**, **forefoot dorsiflexed and abducted**; **rigid rocker-bottom foot** with a **"Persian slipper" appearance**; **palpable talar head on the plantar-medial sole**.
- **About 50% associated with neuromuscular/genetic disorders**: **arthrogryposis**, **myelomeningocele**, **trisomy 13/18**, **prune belly**, **HOXD10 mutation (familial)**; **check the spine, hips, and neurological status**.
- **Diagnostic radiograph: forced (maximal) plantarflexion lateral view**: **the talar axis line stays plantar to the first metatarsal axis (the talonavicular dislocation does not reduce)** (**in congenital oblique talus, it reduces**). **Lateral talar-first metatarsal angle** (Meary) markedly abnormal; **dorsiflexion lateral**: fixed equinus of the calcaneus.
- **Treatment:**
  - **Dobbs method ("reverse Ponseti")**: **serial casting (plantarflexion and inversion: forefoot plantarflexed and inverted with counter-pressure on the talar head)** followed by **percutaneous pinning of the talonavicular joint** (after reduction) and **percutaneous Achilles tenotomy**; **± anterior tibialis transfer to the talar neck**; bracing (**like Ponseti boots**). **Best results**.
  - **Open reduction (single-stage dorsal approach or two-stage) for failed/late cases**: release of the **tibialis anterior, EHL, EDL, peroneus tertius**, dorsal talonavicular capsule; **Achilles lengthening**; **talonavicular pinning**.
  - **Older children: talectomy, subtalar arthrodesis (Grice), triple arthrodesis**.
- **Congenital oblique talus**: **flexible**; **talonavicular joint reduces in plantarflexion**: **casting/observation**.

## 8. Calcaneovalgus foot
- **Postural: foot dorsiflexed, lying against the anterior tibia, hindfoot valgus**: **flexible; intrauterine positioning**; commoner in **first-born girls**; **resolves spontaneously or with stretching (within weeks-months)**.
- **Differential diagnoses:** **CVT** (rigid: radiograph), **posteromedial bowing of the tibia** (**calcaneovalgus foot + posteromedial tibial bowing**: **spontaneous improvement; leg-length discrepancy of about 3-4 cm at maturity: epiphysiodesis/lengthening**), **myelomeningocele (L5)** (weak plantarflexors).

## 9. Flexible flatfoot (pes planovalgus) in children
- **Physiological in infants and toddlers** (**fat pad, ligamentous laxity**; the arch develops by about **6-10 years**).
- **Flexible: arch reconstitutes on tiptoe (Jack/Hubscher toe-raise test), hindfoot inverts on tiptoe**; usually **painless and benign**: **no treatment** (orthoses do not change the natural history).
- **Tight Achilles/gastrocnemius (Silfverskiöld test)** with symptomatic flexible flatfoot: **stretching**; **calcaneal lengthening osteotomy (Evans)** + gastrocnemius recession for **symptomatic, failed conservative care**.
- **Rigid flatfoot:** **tarsal coalition**, **CVT**, **inflammatory arthritis**, **peroneal spastic flatfoot**, **accessory navicular**, **neuromuscular** (cerebral palsy).

## 10. Tarsal coalition
- **Failure of segmentation** (autosomal dominant with variable penetrance) of tarsal bones: **fibrous (syndesmosis), cartilaginous (synchondrosis) or bony (synostosis)**; **about 1-2% (probably higher)**; **bilateral in about 50%**.
- **Calcaneonavicular (CN): commonest (about 53%)**; **presents age 8-12 years** (ossifies earlier); **talocalcaneal (TC; middle facet): about 37%**, **presents age 12-16 years**.
- **Presentation:** **rigid painful flatfoot**, **recurrent ankle sprains**, **peroneal spasm ("peroneal spastic flatfoot")**, **limited subtalar motion**.
- **Radiographs:**
  - **CN coalition: "anteater nose sign" (elongated anterior process of the calcaneus) on lateral**, best seen on the **45-degree internal oblique view**,
  - **TC coalition: "C sign" (continuous line of the talar dome and the sustentaculum)**, **talar beaking (dorsal talar head: traction spur, not arthritis)**, **short talar neck**, best seen on the **Harris (axial) view**; **CT (gold standard; extent of coalition as a percentage of the posterior facet)**.
- **Treatment:**
  - **Non-operative (first): cast/boot immobilisation 4-6 weeks, orthoses, NSAIDs.**
  - **CN coalition: resection with interposition of the extensor digitorum brevis (EDB) or fat** (good results).
  - **TC coalition: resection with fat/FHL interposition if the coalition is under about 50% of the posterior facet area and no significant hindfoot valgus (over about 16-21 degrees) or arthritis**; **otherwise subtalar or triple arthrodesis**; **calcaneal lengthening osteotomy** with resection for valgus.

## 11. Accessory navicular
- **Accessory ossicle at the medial navicular within the tibialis posterior tendon** (**about 10-15% of people**; often bilateral); **Geist/Coughlin types:** **I (os tibiale externum: sesamoid in the tendon)**, **II (synchondrosis: commonest symptomatic)**, **III (cornuate navicular: fused)**.
- **Medial midfoot pain, prominence**, associated with flatfoot.
- **Treatment:** **shoe modification, cast, orthoses**; surgery: **excision of the ossicle ± advancement of the tibialis posterior (Kidner procedure)** or simple excision.

## 12. Cavus foot in children
- **High arch, hindfoot varus**; **two-thirds have an underlying neurological cause**: **Charcot-Marie-Tooth (HMSN type I: commonest; PMP22 duplication on chromosome 17)**, **spinal cord lesions (tethered cord, diastematomyelia, syringomyelia, spinal tumours)**, **Friedreich ataxia**, **polio**, **cerebral palsy**, residual clubfoot. **Unilateral cavus = spinal cord pathology until proved otherwise (MRI spine)**.
- **CMT mechanism:** **weak tibialis anterior vs strong peroneus longus** (**plantarflexed first ray: forefoot-driven cavus**) and **weak peroneus brevis vs strong tibialis posterior** (**hindfoot varus**); **intrinsic weakness (claw toes)**.
- **Coleman block test:** a block under the lateral foot (first ray allowed to drop): **hindfoot varus corrects = flexible hindfoot (forefoot-driven)**: **forefoot surgery (dorsiflexion osteotomy of the first metatarsal) + plantar fascia release ± peroneus longus to brevis transfer** suffices; **does not correct = rigid hindfoot**: add **calcaneal (Dwyer/sliding) osteotomy**; **triple arthrodesis** for severe rigid deformity (avoid if possible: adjacent joint arthritis).
- **Tendon transfers:** **peroneus longus to brevis (balance)**, **tibialis posterior to the dorsum (weak dorsiflexion)**, **Jones transfer (EHL to the first metatarsal neck + IPJ fusion) for clawed hallux**, **Hibbs (EDL to the lateral cuneiform/cuboid)**.

## 13. Toe deformities
- **Curly toes** (3rd-5th; **FDL/FDB tightness**: flexion and medial rotation): **usually resolve; flexor tenotomy** if persistent (**over 3-4 years**).
- **Overlapping fifth toe (digitus minimus varus)**: **dorsal and medial**; symptomatic: **Butler procedure (racquet incision, dorsal capsule release)**.
- **Congenital hallux varus**: **associated with polydactyly, short first metatarsal, longitudinal epiphyseal bracket (delta phalanx)**.
- **Polydactyly (postaxial commonest: fifth toe; African descent)**: excise the duplicated (usually the most lateral/medial) toe at about **9-12 months**.
- **Syndactyly** of toes: no treatment needed (cosmetic).
- **Juvenile/adolescent hallux valgus**: **metatarsus primus varus**, often **family history**, **DMAA increased**; **delay surgery until skeletal maturity** (**recurrence is high when physes are open**); **hemiepiphysiodesis of the lateral first metatarsal physis** (guided growth) in younger children.
- **Köhler disease** (**osteochondrosis of the navicular**, **boys aged 4-6**; **sclerotic, flattened navicular**; **self-limiting**: **short leg walking cast 6-8 weeks** shortens symptoms).
- **Freiberg infraction** (**osteochondrosis of the second metatarsal head**, **adolescent girls**; **Smillie stages I-V**; rest, stiff-soled shoes; **dorsal closing-wedge osteotomy** (Gauthier), debridement).
- **Sever disease** (**calcaneal apophysitis**, **ages 8-12**, **active children**: **heel pain with activity**, **squeeze test**: **self-limiting**: heel cups, stretching, activity modification).

> Exam pearl: **Clubfoot = CAVE; corrected in that order. Ponseti: supinate to correct cavus; abduct with counter-pressure on the lateral talar head (not the CC joint: Kite's error); Achilles tenotomy in about 80-90%; braces 23 h/day for 3 months then nights until 4-5 years. Non-compliance with bracing = commonest cause of relapse; dynamic supination = TATT to the lateral cuneiform.**

> Exam pearl: **Talar neck = most deformed bone; navicular medially subluxed; anterior tibial artery often absent. Pirani score (MFCS + HFCS, max 6). Pronation during Ponseti = rocker-bottom foot.**

> Exam pearl: **CVT: rigid rocker-bottom; plantarflexion lateral view: talonavicular dislocation persists (oblique talus reduces); 50% syndromic; Dobbs reverse Ponseti + TN pinning + tenotomy. Metatarsus adductus: normal hindfoot, no equinus, mostly resolves. Skewfoot = adductus + hindfoot valgus.**

> Exam pearl: **Tarsal coalition: CN (anteater nose, 8-12 years, 45-degree oblique) vs TC (C sign, talar beak, 12-16 years, CT); resect with EDB interposition (CN) or fat (TC under 50% facet). Unilateral cavus = spinal MRI; bilateral cavus = CMT; Coleman block test decides hindfoot surgery. Köhler navicular (self-limiting), Freiberg 2nd MT head, Sever calcaneal apophysitis.**

paediatric fractures.md:
## 1. Why children's fractures are different
- **Periosteum** is thick, strong and osteogenic: it limits displacement, acts as a hinge for reduction (keep the intact periosteal side as the hinge) and produces fast, abundant callus.
- **Bone is more porous and less brittle:** it fails in compression (**torus/buckle**), on the tension side only (**greenstick**), or bends without fracture (**plastic deformation**, most often ulna and fibula; can block reduction of the partner bone).
- **Remodelling** is greatest when the child is young, the fracture is **near a fast-growing physis**, and the deformity is **in the plane of motion of the adjacent joint**. **Rotational deformity does not remodel.** Intra-articular step-off does not remodel.
- **Overgrowth:** femoral shaft fractures in children aged about 2-10 overgrow by roughly 1-2 cm, which is why 1-2 cm of shortening (overlap) is accepted in a spica.
- **Ligaments are stronger than the physis:** an apparent "sprain" in a child is often a physeal injury (e.g. Salter-Harris I of the distal fibula).
- **Fastest-growing physes:** proximal humerus (about 80% of humeral growth) and distal radius (about 75-80% of radial growth) in the upper limb; **distal femur (about 70% of femoral length)** and proximal tibia (about 55-60% of tibial length) around the knee. Roughly 1 cm a year at the distal femur and 0.6 cm at the proximal tibia.

## 2. The physis and Salter-Harris
- **Zones (epiphysis to metaphysis):** reserve (resting), proliferative, **hypertrophic** (maturation, degeneration, **provisional calcification**). Fractures usually propagate through the hypertrophic zone, the weakest region; the germinal (reserve and proliferative) cells stay with the epiphysis, which is why most physeal fractures grow normally.
- **Salter-Harris classification:**

| Type | Fracture line | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| I | Through the physis only | Infants and young children; radiographs may be normal (look for widening); distal fibula, proximal humerus in neonates |
| **II** | Physis + metaphyseal fragment (**Thurston-Holland**) | **Commonest (about 75%)**; the periosteum is intact on the fragment side |
| III | Physis + epiphysis (intra-articular) | Needs anatomical reduction (e.g. juvenile Tillaux) |
| IV | Metaphysis + physis + epiphysis | Intra-articular and crosses the germinal layer; **ORIF**; high risk of a bar (e.g. medial malleolus, lateral condyle humerus) |
| V | Crush of the physis | Usually diagnosed retrospectively when growth arrest appears; worst prognosis |
| VI (Rang) | Perichondral ring injury | Peripheral bar, angular deformity (lawnmower injuries) |

- **Peterson type I** (transverse metaphyseal fracture extending into the physis, distal radius) is worth knowing for FET-level questions.
- **Highest growth-disturbance risk:** **distal femur** (even SH I and II, because of the undulating physis), proximal tibia, distal tibia SH III/IV.
- **Physeal bar:** diagnose with **MRI (or CT) mapping**. Resect with interposition (fat, cement) if it involves **under 50%** of the physis and the child has **at least 2 years (about 2 cm) of growth left**. Otherwise complete the arrest (epiphysiodesis), deal with the other bone, and correct the angulation and length.
- **Park-Harris growth arrest lines** that converge on the physis indicate a bar; parallel lines mean symmetrical growth.

## 3. Elbow (the high-yield region)
### Ossification centres (CRITOE)
- **C**apitellum about 1 year, **R**adial head 3-5, **I**nternal (medial) epicondyle 5-7, **T**rochlea 7-9, **O**lecranon 9-11, **E**xternal (lateral) epicondyle 11-13 (girls earlier).
- The **medial epicondyle always appears before the trochlea**: an ossified fragment in the joint before the trochlea ossifies is an incarcerated medial epicondyle.
- **Anterior humeral line** passes through the middle third of the capitellum; the **radiocapitellar line** passes through the capitellum in every view (if not, look for Monteggia).
- **Posterior fat pad sign** = effusion = occult fracture (supracondylar, lateral condyle, radial neck).

### Supracondylar humerus fracture
- Commonest elbow fracture in children (peak 5-7 years), mechanism fall on the outstretched hand. **Extension type about 97%**, flexion type about 3%.
- **Gartland classification (with Wilkins modification):**

| Type | Description | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| I | Undisplaced; posterior fat pad only | Above-elbow cast 3 weeks |
| IIA | Displaced, posterior cortex intact (hinge), no rotation | Closed reduction; pin if anterior humeral line misses the capitellum |
| IIB | Hinged but rotated or translated | Closed reduction and pinning |
| III | Completely displaced | **Closed reduction and percutaneous pinning** |
| IV (Leitch) | Multidirectionally unstable (periosteal hinge lost) | Pinning; often diagnosed under the image intensifier |

- **Nerves:** **anterior interosseous nerve is the commonest** (extension type), then radial, median and ulnar.
  - **Posterolateral displacement** of the distal fragment (proximal spike goes anteromedial): **median nerve and brachial artery**.
  - **Posteromedial displacement** (spike goes anterolateral): **radial nerve**.
  - **Flexion type:** **ulnar nerve**.
  - **Iatrogenic:** ulnar nerve with a medial pin, especially when the elbow is hyperflexed (the nerve subluxes anteriorly).
  - Most nerve palsies are neurapraxias that recover in 2-3 months.
- **Pinning:** **2 or 3 divergent lateral pins** separated at the fracture site are stable for most fractures with no ulnar nerve risk. Crossed pins are biomechanically stiffer; if a medial pin is needed, make a small incision and extend the elbow before placing it.
- **Vascular status:**
  - **Pink pulseless hand** (perfused, no palpable pulse) after reduction: admit, elevate and observe closely. Explore only if perfusion deteriorates or there is **associated median nerve palsy** (the artery may be tethered or entrapped).
  - **White pulseless hand** after closed reduction: **urgent open exploration** of the brachial artery (anterior approach).
  - **Compartment syndrome** (Volkmann ischaemia) risk is higher with ipsilateral forearm fracture (floating elbow) and with **casting in more than 90 degrees of flexion**.
- **Assessing reduction:** **Baumann angle** (shaft axis vs capitellar physis on AP; about 70-75 degrees, compare with the other side; change over 5 degrees = coronal malalignment), anterior humeral line, **teardrop**, medial and lateral column integrity.
- **Cubitus varus ("gunstock")** is the commonest late complication. It is due to **malunion (medial column collapse, internal rotation)**, not growth disturbance. It is cosmetic but can cause posterolateral rotatory instability, ulnar nerve symptoms and snapping triceps. Treat with a **lateral closing-wedge (French) osteotomy** or dome osteotomy.

### Lateral condyle fracture
- Second commonest elbow fracture (age 5-10). It is **intra-articular and physeal (behaves like SH IV)**, pulled by the extensor muscles, so it displaces and has a high **non-union** risk.
- **Milch I** (lateral to the trochlear groove, SH IV, stable elbow) vs **Milch II** (into the trochlear groove, SH II-like, elbow unstable). **Jakob/Weiss** grade by displacement: under 2 mm, 2-4 mm with intact cartilage hinge, over 4 mm and rotated.
- **Internal oblique view** shows the true displacement best. An **arthrogram or MRI** shows whether the articular cartilage hinge is intact.
- **Treatment:** under 2 mm, cast with weekly radiographs (it can displace); **over 2 mm, ORIF** (posterior dissection is avoided: the blood supply enters posteriorly, so dissecting there causes **AVN of the condyle**).
- **Complications:** non-union, leading to **cubitus valgus** and **tardy ulnar nerve palsy** years later; lateral spur (overgrowth, cosmetic "pseudo-varus"); fishtail deformity.

### Medial epicondyle fracture
- Ages 9-14; a traction (apophyseal) injury; about half are associated with **elbow dislocation**.
- **Absolute indication for surgery: incarceration of the fragment in the joint** (after dislocation reduction). Relative: ulnar nerve dysfunction, valgus instability in throwers or gymnasts, displacement in the dominant arm of an athlete.
- Most displaced fractures do well non-operatively (fibrous union is usually painless).

### Radial neck, Monteggia and other forearm injuries
- **Radial neck:** angulation **under 30 degrees** is accepted; 30-60 degrees, closed reduction (Patterson manoeuvre, Israeli technique); over 60 degrees or translated, percutaneous joystick or **intramedullary (Metaizeau) reduction**. Avoid open reduction where possible: **loss of forearm rotation (stiffness) is the commonest complication**, and AVN of the radial head and radioulnar synostosis follow open reduction.
- **Monteggia (Bado):** I anterior radial head dislocation with apex-anterior ulnar fracture (**commonest in children**), II posterior, III lateral (often ulnar metaphyseal greenstick), IV anterior dislocation with both-bone fracture. In children, **restoring ulnar length and alignment usually reduces the radial head**; plastic deformation of the ulna must be corrected. A **missed Monteggia** (chronic) needs ulnar osteotomy with annular ligament reconstruction.
- **Galeazzi:** radial shaft fracture with distal radioulnar joint disruption; the paediatric equivalent is a distal ulnar physeal separation.
- **Forearm shaft:** acceptable alignment is generous in children under about 9 (angulation up to about 15 degrees, bayonet apposition, malrotation up to about 45 degrees); in older children less (about 10 degrees angulation, 30 degrees malrotation). Mid-shaft radius malunion limits rotation most. **Elastic stable intramedullary nails** for unstable fractures in older children. **Refracture** is common (about 5%) after greenstick fractures: complete the greenstick or cast long enough.
- **Distal radius:** the commonest paediatric fracture overall. Huge remodelling capacity: in a child with 2 years of growth left, up to about 20-25 degrees of sagittal angulation is acceptable. **Do not re-manipulate a physeal (SH II) fracture after 5-7 days** (physeal damage).
- **Nursemaid's elbow (pulled elbow):** annular ligament subluxation in children aged 1-4. Reduce by supination with flexion or by hyperpronation (more successful).

## 4. Proximal humerus and clavicle
- Proximal humerus physeal fractures (SH II in adolescents, SH I in younger children) remodel enormously (up to about 60 degrees accepted in young children). Operate only in adolescents with severe displacement or soft-tissue interposition (biceps tendon).
- **Neonatal clavicle fracture** (difficult delivery, pseudoparalysis): heals without treatment. Differentiate from **obstetric brachial plexus palsy** and **congenital pseudarthrosis of the clavicle** (right side, painless, no callus, subclavian artery pressure theory).
- **Medial clavicle physeal injury** (the last physis to close, about 23-25 years): posterior displacement can compress mediastinal structures. **CT**, then reduce in theatre with a thoracic surgeon available.

## 5. Spine in children
- **SCIWORA** (spinal cord injury without radiographic abnormality) is due to the elastic paediatric spine; **MRI** shows the lesion.
- Upper cervical injuries predominate under about 8 years (large head, horizontal facets). **Pseudosubluxation of C2 on C3** (up to about 4 mm) is normal; use the **Swischuk line**.
- Use a **back-board with an occipital recess or shoulder roll** in children under about 6 (the large occiput flexes the neck).
- **Chance (flexion-distraction) fracture** with a lap belt: look for associated **bowel injury**.

## 6. Pelvis and hip
- Pelvic fractures in children often need less fixation (elastic pelvis), but **associated visceral injuries** are frequent. The triradiate cartilage can arrest (shallow acetabulum).
- **Avulsion fractures in adolescent athletes:** ASIS (sartorius), **AIIS (rectus femoris)**, ischial tuberosity (**hamstrings**, the one that may need fixation if displaced over 1.5-2 cm), lesser trochanter (iliopsoas; **in an adult, a lesser trochanter avulsion = pathological fracture until proved otherwise**).
- **Delbet classification of paediatric hip fractures:**

| Type | Site | Frequency | AVN risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | Transepiphyseal (with or without dislocation) | Rare | Highest, near 100% with dislocation |
| **II** | **Transcervical** | **Commonest (about 45-50%)** | About 50% |
| III | Cervicotrochanteric (basicervical) | About 30% | About 25% |
| IV | Intertrochanteric | About 10-15% | Lowest, about 10% |

- Treat as an emergency: **urgent anatomical reduction**, stable fixation (avoid crossing the physis if possible in young children; stability is more important than sparing it), and **capsular decompression**. Complications: **AVN (commonest and most serious)**, coxa vara, non-union, premature physeal closure.

## 7. Femoral shaft
| Age / size | Treatment |
|---|---|
| **0-6 months** | **Pavlik harness** or posterior splint |
| **6 months-5 years** | **Immediate (or early) hip spica**; accept up to about 2 cm shortening, about 15 degrees varus/valgus and about 20 degrees anterior/posterior angulation (less with age) |
| **5-11 years** | **Flexible (titanium) elastic nails** for length-stable fractures in children **under about 45-49 kg**; submuscular bridge plating or external fixation for length-unstable or comminuted fractures |
| **Over about 11 years or heavier** | **Rigid intramedullary nail through a lateral trochanteric entry**. Avoid piriformis entry: the lateral ascending cervical branches of the **medial femoral circumflex artery** pass there, so it risks **AVN of the femoral head** |

- **Elastic nails:** two nails, each about **40% of the medullary canal diameter** (combined about 80%), pre-bent to the same curve so they balance. **Complications:** loss of length in unstable patterns, nail-end irritation, malunion in heavier children.
- A **femoral fracture in a child who is not yet walking** (under about 1 year) is a red flag for **non-accidental injury**.
- **Distal femoral physeal fractures** (often SH II) have a high rate of growth arrest (about 40-50%) even when well treated: warn the family and follow up for 1-2 years.

## 8. Knee
- **Tibial spine (eminence) fracture:** ages 8-14, the paediatric ACL equivalent. **Meyers-McKeever:** I undisplaced, II anterior hinge, III completely displaced (IIIA displaced, IIIB rotated), IV comminuted (Zaricznyj). The **intermeniscal ligament or anterior horn of the medial meniscus** can block reduction. Type I and reducible II: long-leg cast in extension. Irreducible II, III and IV: **arthroscopic or open reduction and fixation** (suture or screw).
- **Tibial tubercle avulsion:** adolescent boys jumping; Ogden classification. Watch for **compartment syndrome** (anterior tibial recurrent artery).
- **Patellar sleeve fracture:** a cartilage sleeve pulled off the inferior pole (ages 8-12); the radiograph shows only a small fleck of bone and patella alta, so the injury is underestimated. ORIF.
- **Proximal tibial metaphyseal fracture (Cozen):** a seemingly innocent undisplaced fracture in a child aged 3-6 develops **progressive genu valgum** over the next year from asymmetric overgrowth. Warn the parents; most remodel; avoid early osteotomy.
- **Proximal tibial physeal (SH) fractures:** risk of **popliteal artery injury** (the artery is tethered at the trifurcation).

## 9. Tibia and ankle
- **Toddler's fracture:** undisplaced spiral fracture of the distal tibia in a child just walking (9 months-3 years). May only show on an oblique view or at 10-14 days. Usually accidental.
- **Transitional fractures** occur in adolescents, because the distal tibial physis closes over about 18 months: **central first, then medial, then lateral**.
  - **Juvenile Tillaux:** SH III avulsion of the **anterolateral epiphysis** by the **anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament**, as only the lateral physis is still open.
  - **Triplane:** SH IV in three planes. It looks like SH III on the AP view and SH II on the lateral view; two-, three- or four-part types.
  - **CT** for both. **Articular displacement over 2 mm** needs reduction and fixation (screws parallel to the joint, avoiding the physis if growth remains).
- **Distal tibial SH III/IV (medial malleolus):** high risk of physeal bar and **varus** deformity. Anatomical ORIF.

## 10. Non-accidental injury (NAI)
- Red flags: a history inconsistent with the injury or the child's development, delay in presentation, injuries of different ages, and **any fracture in a non-ambulant infant**.
- **High-specificity fractures:** **classic metaphyseal lesions** (corner or bucket-handle fractures, from shaking or twisting), **posterior rib fractures** (squeezing), scapula, spinous process and sternum fractures.
- Moderate specificity: multiple or bilateral fractures, fractures of different ages, epiphyseal separations, vertebral body fractures, digital fractures in non-ambulant children, complex skull fractures.
- **Commonest fracture in abuse overall: diaphyseal long-bone fracture** (humerus or femur in infants); **humeral shaft fracture under 3 years** is suspicious.
- **Workup:** full **skeletal survey** in children under 2 (repeat at about 2 weeks), ophthalmology (retinal haemorrhages), head imaging, bloods (bone profile, vitamin D, coagulation). Differentials: **osteogenesis imperfecta**, rickets, scurvy, Caffey disease, congenital syphilis, normal metaphyseal variants.
- The treating doctor has a duty to **report concerns** (in India: child protection services; POCSO where sexual abuse is suspected) and to admit the child for safety.

> Exam pearl: **AIN is the commonest nerve injured in a supracondylar fracture; the ulnar nerve is the commonest iatrogenic injury (medial pin).** A **lateral condyle fracture over 2 mm displaced needs ORIF**, and its late complication is **tardy ulnar palsy from cubitus valgus**.

> Exam pearl: **Delbet II is the commonest paediatric hip fracture; Delbet I has the highest AVN risk.** **Piriformis-entry nails are avoided in children because of AVN.**

cerebral palsy and neuromuscular.md:
## 1. Cerebral palsy: definition and classification
- A group of permanent disorders of movement and posture caused by a **non-progressive lesion of the immature brain** (before, during or within about 2 years after birth). The brain lesion is static, but the **musculoskeletal problems are progressive** (muscles do not grow at the rate of bone under spasticity, so contractures and bony deformity develop with growth).
- **Risk factors:** prematurity and low birth weight (strongest), perinatal hypoxia, intrauterine infection, multiple pregnancy, kernicterus (athetoid CP), neonatal stroke.
- **Physiological classification:**
  - **Spastic** (about 70-80%; upper motor neurone, velocity-dependent tone; pyramidal tract).
  - **Dyskinetic** (athetosis, dystonia, chorea; basal ganglia; kernicterus). **Poor candidates for tendon surgery** (unpredictable results).
  - **Ataxic** (cerebellum).
  - Mixed.
- **Topographic classification:** **hemiplegia** (arm worse than leg; walks by about 18-24 months; seizures common), **diplegia** (legs much worse than arms; classic for prematurity with **periventricular leukomalacia**), **quadriplegia / total body involvement** (all limbs, poor head control, intellectual disability, seizures, feeding problems).
- **GMFCS (Gross Motor Function Classification System), age 6-12 descriptors:**

| Level | Function |
|---|---|
| I | Walks without limitation; difficulty only with advanced skills |
| II | Walks with limitations (long distances, uneven ground, stairs need a rail) |
| III | Walks with a hand-held mobility device (walker, crutches); wheelchair for long distances |
| IV | Self-mobility limited; powered mobility; may walk short distances with assistance |
| V | Transported in a manual wheelchair; very limited head and trunk control |

- GMFCS is stable over time and predicts **hip displacement risk** (about 0% at level I to about 90% at level V) and walking prognosis.
- **Walking prognosis:** sitting independently by **age 2** predicts walking; not sitting by 4 suggests the child will not walk. Persistent primitive reflexes after age 1 (Bleck's criteria) are poor signs.

## 2. Principles of management
- **Team approach:** physiotherapy, orthoses, tone management, orthopaedic surgery. Goals depend on GMFCS: improve gait in I-III; keep sitting comfortable, hips painless, and spine balanced in IV-V.
- **Tone management:**
  - **Botulinum toxin A** (blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction) for focal **dynamic** spasticity in young children (typically 2-6), effect lasts about 3-6 months. Combine with serial casting. Not useful for fixed contracture.
  - **Oral baclofen** (GABA-B agonist; sedation limits use); **intrathecal baclofen pump** for severe generalised spasticity or dystonia (GMFCS IV-V).
  - **Selective dorsal rhizotomy (SDR):** sectioning a proportion (often about half) of the L2-S1 dorsal rootlets, guided by intraoperative stimulation. Ideal candidate: **spastic diplegia, GMFCS II-III, age about 4-8**, good strength and selective motor control, minimal fixed contractures, no dystonia. Permanent reduction of spasticity; may unmask weakness; later hip subluxation and spinal deformity can occur.
- **Gait analysis** (3D kinematics, kinetics, EMG) before multilevel surgery.
- **Single-event multilevel surgery (SEMLS):** correct all soft-tissue and bony deformities in one operation (rather than "birthday syndrome" of one operation a year), typically at **age about 6-10** when gait has matured. Followed by intensive rehabilitation for about a year.

## 3. The hip in CP
- **Spastic hip displacement** is due to overactive **adductors and iliopsoas** with weak abductors and extensors, leading to **coxa valga, increased femoral anteversion, and acetabular dysplasia (posterosuperior)**. The hip subluxes **posterosuperiorly** (unlike DDH).
- **Hip surveillance:** clinical exam and AP pelvis radiograph from about age 2, every 6-12 months, more often for GMFCS III-V (Australian/CPUP-based protocols).
- **Reimers migration percentage (MP):** percentage of the femoral head width lateral to Perkin's line. Normal under about 10%; **over 30-40% = subluxation**; 100% = dislocation. **Progression over about 10% a year** is significant.
- **Management by severity:**

| Situation | Surgery |
|---|---|
| Young child (under about 6-8), **MP 30-40%** (some use 25-60%) | **Preventive soft-tissue release:** adductor longus and gracilis tenotomy ± iliopsoas lengthening (psoas over brim) |
| **MP over 40-50%, older child, or failed release** | **Reconstructive:** **varus derotation osteotomy (VDRO)** of the proximal femur ± **pelvic osteotomy (Dega or San Diego)** for acetabular dysplasia, with open reduction if needed |
| **Painful, long-standing dislocation with arthritic head** in a non-walker | **Salvage:** proximal femoral resection (Castle or McHale), valgus osteotomy (Schanz), arthrodesis or arthroplasty |

- Do not do an isolated obturator neurectomy (anterior branch) routinely; abandoned by most because of over-abduction (windswept or abduction contracture).
- **Windswept hips:** one hip abducted, the other adducted and dislocated, with pelvic obliquity and scoliosis.

## 4. The knee in CP
- **Crouch gait** (excessive knee flexion in stance): due to hamstring contracture, weak soleus or plantarflexor-knee-extension couple insufficiency (often **after isolated over-lengthening of the Achilles tendon**), lever-arm dysfunction (external tibial torsion, foot instability). Treat with hamstring lengthening, correction of lever arms, **distal femoral extension osteotomy** with **patellar tendon advancement** in severe fixed crouch, and floor-reaction AFOs.
- **Stiff-knee gait:** reduced and delayed knee flexion in swing from an **overactive rectus femoris** (confirmed by dynamic EMG; Duncan-Ely test). Treat with **distal rectus femoris transfer** (to the semitendinosus or gracilis) rather than release.
- **Hamstring tightness:** popliteal angle increased. Medial hamstring lengthening; lateral lengthening only if needed (risk of recurvatum and crouch). **Hamstring lengthening increases anterior pelvic tilt** (the hamstrings are hip extensors too).
- **Jump gait** (equinus + knee and hip flexion) and **true equinus** (hemiplegia). The Rodda and Graham sagittal gait classification: true equinus, jump, apparent equinus, crouch.

## 5. The foot in CP
- **Equinus** is the commonest deformity.
  - **Silfverskiold test:** if dorsiflexion improves with the knee flexed, the **gastrocnemius alone** is tight: **gastrocnemius recession** (Strayer, Vulpius, Baker). If not, both are tight: **tendo-Achilles lengthening** (Hoke triple hemisection, Z-lengthening).
  - **Avoid over-lengthening the Achilles tendon** in diplegia: it causes **crouch gait**, which is far worse than mild equinus. Diplegic equinus is often "apparent" (from knee and hip flexion).
- **Equinovarus** (hemiplegia): overactive **tibialis posterior** (split posterior tibial tendon transfer, SPLATT-type to peroneus brevis, or lengthening) or **tibialis anterior** (split anterior tibial tendon transfer, **SPLATT**). Confirm the culprit with dynamic EMG.
- **Equinovalgus / planovalgus** (diplegia and quadriplegia): peroneal overactivity and gastrocnemius-soleus contracture. **Calcaneal lengthening osteotomy (Evans)** in mobile feet; **subtalar or triple arthrodesis** in rigid or severe feet in older children.
- **Hallux valgus** develops with planovalgus: first MTP arthrodesis.

## 6. Spine and upper limb in CP
- **Neuromuscular scoliosis:** long **C-shaped thoracolumbar curves** with **pelvic obliquity**, mainly in GMFCS IV-V. Progresses even after skeletal maturity (especially curves over about 40 degrees).
- **Posterior spinal fusion from T2 to the pelvis** (pelvic fixation with iliac or **S2-alar-iliac** screws) when the curve exceeds about 40-50 degrees and sitting balance worsens. Complications are higher than in idiopathic scoliosis: infection, blood loss, pulmonary problems. Optimise nutrition first.
- **Upper limb (hemiplegia):** shoulder internal rotation, elbow flexion, forearm pronation, wrist and finger flexion, **thumb-in-palm**. Surgery (e.g. **flexor carpi ulnaris to ECRB transfer**, pronator teres rerouting, thumb adductor release) mainly improves function and hygiene; needs good sensation and voluntary control (the House and Zancolli classifications).

## 7. Muscular dystrophies
### Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD)
- **X-linked recessive**, absent **dystrophin** (Xp21; deletions in about 65%); one-third are new mutations. Boys; incidence about 1 in 3,500-5,000 male births.
- Presents at **3-5 years**: clumsiness, frequent falls, **toe-walking**, **Gowers sign** (climbing up the thighs to stand: proximal weakness), **calf pseudohypertrophy** (fat and fibrous replacement), waddling gait, lumbar lordosis.
- **CK massively raised** (10-100 times normal, even at birth); diagnosis by **genetic testing** (multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification); muscle biopsy (absent dystrophin on immunostaining) if needed.
- **Natural history:** loss of walking around **age 12** (later on steroids), scoliosis after loss of ambulation, death in the 20s-30s from **cardiomyopathy** or respiratory failure.
- **Corticosteroids** (prednisolone or deflazacort) prolong walking by about 2-3 years, reduce scoliosis and improve cardiorespiratory function. Exon-skipping drugs (e.g. eteplirsen for exon 51) and gene therapy for selected mutations.
- **Orthopaedics:** keep walking as long as possible (Achilles and ITB releases with KAFOs in selected cases). **Scoliosis:** fuse **early**, when the curve is **about 20-30 degrees**, before the **FVC falls below about 30-35%** (anaesthetic risk rises sharply). Long fusion to the pelvis or L5. **Malignant hyperthermia-like reactions** and rhabdomyolysis: avoid succinylcholine and volatile agents.
- Fractures from osteoporosis (steroids, immobility): treat quickly to keep walking.

### Becker and other dystrophies
- **Becker:** reduced or abnormal dystrophin; later onset (over about 7), walks beyond 16, milder, cardiomyopathy common.
- **Limb-girdle** (autosomal), **facioscapulohumeral** (AD; scapular winging, facial weakness: **scapulothoracic fusion** for winging), **Emery-Dreifuss** (early **elbow flexion contractures**, Achilles contracture, **cardiac conduction block**: pacemaker).
- **Myotonic dystrophy** (CTG repeat; distal weakness, myotonia, cataracts, frontal balding, cardiac conduction defects).

## 8. Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA)
- Autosomal recessive **SMN1 deletion**, loss of **anterior horn cells**: symmetric proximal weakness, absent reflexes, tongue fasciculation, **normal sensation and intelligence**. SMN2 copy number modifies severity.
- **Types:** I (Werdnig-Hoffmann; never sits, death in infancy without treatment), II (sits but never stands), III (Kugelberg-Welander; walks), IV adult.
- **Nusinersen** (antisense oligonucleotide, intrathecal), **onasemnogene abeparvovec** (gene therapy) and **risdiplam** (oral) have transformed survival.
- **Scoliosis** almost universal in type II: bracing for sitting, then **growth-friendly instrumentation** (growing rods, magnetically controlled) or fusion; leave access for intrathecal therapy if possible.
- **Hip subluxation and dislocation** are common but usually **painless: leave them alone**.

## 9. Myelomeningocele (spina bifida)
- Folic acid deficiency, valproate. Associated **Arnold-Chiari II malformation, hydrocephalus (shunt)**, tethered cord, syringomyelia, neurogenic bladder, **latex allergy** (latex-free theatre).
- **Motor level determines function:**

| Level | Key muscle working | Typical function |
|---|---|---|
| Thoracic / L1-L2 | Hip flexors only | Wheelchair; standing in a frame |
| **L3-L4** | **Quadriceps (L3-4), tibialis anterior (L4)** | Household or community walker with AFOs/crutches; **functional quadriceps is the key to walking** |
| L5 | Hamstrings, toe extensors, gluteus medius partly | Community walker, AFOs |
| Sacral | Gastrocnemius-soleus | Near-normal walking |

- **Hip dislocation** is commonest at L3-L4 (unopposed hip flexors and adductors vs weak abductors and extensors). **Do not reduce** a dislocated hip in most cases; correct contractures to keep the pelvis level.
- **Rapidly increasing scoliosis, new spasticity, deteriorating gait, changing foot deformity or urinary function:** suspect **tethered cord, shunt malfunction or syrinx**; MRI and neurosurgical review.
- **Feet:** aim for a **plantigrade, braceable foot**. Rigid clubfoot (talectomy in severe cases), vertical talus, calcaneus foot (L4-L5; anterior tibial transfer to the calcaneus). **Insensate feet** develop pressure ulcers and Charcot changes.
- **Fractures** in insensate limbs present as warm, swollen limbs with fever (mistaken for infection) and heal with exuberant callus.

## 10. Hereditary neuropathies and other conditions
- **Charcot-Marie-Tooth (HMSN):** commonest inherited neuropathy. **Type 1A: PMP22 duplication on chromosome 17**, demyelinating, slow conduction velocities. Type 2: axonal.
  - **Cavovarus foot**, claw toes, peroneal muscle wasting ("**inverted champagne bottle**" legs), intrinsic hand weakness.
  - **Mechanism:** weak **tibialis anterior** is overpowered by **peroneus longus** (plantarflexed first ray, forefoot-driven cavus); weak **peroneus brevis** is overpowered by **tibialis posterior** (hindfoot varus).
  - **Coleman block test:** a block under the lateral forefoot lets the first ray drop; if the **hindfoot varus corrects**, the hindfoot is flexible and the deformity is forefoot driven: plantar fascia release, **first metatarsal dorsiflexion osteotomy**, **peroneus longus to brevis transfer**, ± tibialis posterior transfer. If not, add a **lateralising calcaneal osteotomy**; triple arthrodesis only for rigid, arthritic feet.
- **Friedreich ataxia:** AR, **GAA trinucleotide repeat in frataxin** (chromosome 9). Ataxia from about age 10, areflexia, cavovarus feet, scoliosis (more like idiopathic in shape), **hypertrophic cardiomyopathy** (the main cause of death), diabetes.
- **Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita:** multiple **non-progressive** congenital contractures, normal sensation and usually normal intelligence. **Amyoplasia** (classic): internally rotated shoulders, extended elbows, flexed wrists, rigid **clubfeet**, dislocated hips, knee contractures. Early stretching; surgery aims for walking and independent function (bilateral hip dislocations are usually left; unilateral may be reduced).
- **Poliomyelitis (residual paralysis)** is still examined in India: asymmetric flaccid paralysis with normal sensation; tendon transfers once power has plateaued (about 2 years), "**a muscle loses one grade of power after transfer**", and transfer **in phase** where possible.

> Exam pearl: **Silfverskiold test positive = gastrocnemius recession; over-lengthening the Achilles in a diplegic child causes crouch gait.** **Stiff-knee gait = distal rectus femoris transfer.**

> Exam pearl: **DMD scoliosis: fuse early (curve about 20-30 degrees, FVC above about 30-35%).** **SMA hip dislocation: leave alone.** **Myelomeningocele: L3-L4 (quadriceps) is the key level for walking.**

skeletal dysplasias.md:
## 1. Approach to a short child
- **Proportionate short stature:** constitutional, familial, endocrine (hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency), nutritional, systemic disease.
- **Disproportionate short stature = skeletal dysplasia** until proved otherwise:
  - **Short-limbed** (achondroplasia, pseudoachondroplasia, metaphyseal dysplasias) vs **short-trunk** (spondyloepiphyseal dysplasias, Morquio).
  - Pattern of limb shortening: **rhizomelic** (proximal: humerus and femur; achondroplasia), **mesomelic** (forearm and leg; Langer, dyschondrosteosis/Leri-Weill with **Madelung deformity**, SHOX gene), **acromelic** (hands and feet).
- Radiographic approach: which part of the bone is affected? **Epiphyseal** (MED, SED), **metaphyseal** (achondroplasia, metaphyseal chondrodysplasias, rickets), **diaphyseal** (Camurati-Engelmann), and is the **spine** involved (spondylo-)?
- **Upper cervical instability screen** (flexion-extension films ± MRI) before anaesthesia in **Morquio, SED congenita, pseudoachondroplasia, Down syndrome, Larsen syndrome, metatropic dysplasia**.

## 2. FGFR3 group
- **FGFR3 is a negative regulator of chondrocyte proliferation:** activating (gain-of-function) mutations slow growth at the physis.
- **Achondroplasia** (commonest skeletal dysplasia, about 1 in 25,000):
  - **Autosomal dominant**, **FGFR3 G380R** (Gly380Arg) in about 98%; **about 80% are new mutations** associated with **advanced paternal age**. Homozygous achondroplasia is lethal.
  - **Clinical:** rhizomelic shortening, **frontal bossing**, midface hypoplasia, **trident hand** (separation of middle and ring fingers), **genu varum** (fibular overgrowth), thoracolumbar kyphosis in infancy (usually resolves when walking), lumbar hyperlordosis, normal trunk length, normal intelligence. Average adult height about 125-130 cm.
  - **Radiographs:** **interpedicular distance narrows from L1 to L5** (normally widens), short pedicles, posterior vertebral scalloping, **champagne-glass pelvic inlet**, squared iliac wings, flat acetabular roofs, inverted-V physes at the knee.
  - **Spine problems:** **foramen magnum stenosis** in infancy (central apnoea, hypotonia, **sudden death**; screen with MRI/polysomnography; suboccipital decompression); **thoracolumbar kyphosis** (avoid unsupported sitting; bracing; fusion if progressive over about 30 degrees after age 3-5); **lumbar spinal stenosis in adults** (neurogenic claudication; wide laminectomy and fusion).
  - **Genu varum:** osteotomy or guided growth if symptomatic. Limb lengthening is controversial.
  - **Vosoritide** (C-type natriuretic peptide analogue; antagonises FGFR3 signalling) increases annual growth velocity.
- **Hypochondroplasia** (FGFR3, milder; normal face). **Thanatophoric dysplasia** (FGFR3; lethal; "telephone-receiver" femora, cloverleaf skull).

## 3. COMP and type IX collagen group
- **Pseudoachondroplasia** (COMP, cartilage oligomeric matrix protein; AD):
  - **Normal face and normal length at birth**; short limbs become apparent at **2-3 years**.
  - Marked **ligamentous laxity**, windswept knees, **odontoid hypoplasia with C1-C2 instability**, small irregular epiphyses, flared metaphyses, early **osteoarthritis** of hips and knees.
  - Distinguish from achondroplasia: normal face and skull, normal interpedicular distance.
- **Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (MED)** (COMP, type IX collagen COL9A1-3, matrilin-3; usually AD):
  - Mild short stature, joint pain and stiffness, **small, irregular, flattened epiphyses**, **double-layered patella** (recessive type, SLC26A2).
  - **Bilateral, symmetrical femoral head changes at the same stage**, normal spine, acetabular involvement: differentiates it from **bilateral Perthes** (asynchronous, different stages).
  - **Premature osteoarthritis**: hip arthroplasty in early adulthood.

## 4. Type II collagen group (COL2A1)
- Type II collagen is in **articular cartilage, physis, vitreous humour and the inner ear**, which explains the eye and hearing problems.
- **Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia (SED) congenita** (AD, COL2A1):
  - **Short-trunk** dwarfism present at birth, barrel chest, **coxa vara**, **odontoid hypoplasia / os odontoideum with atlantoaxial instability** (fuse C1-C2 if instability or myelopathy), kyphoscoliosis.
  - **Myopia and retinal detachment** (annual eye examination), hearing loss, cleft palate.
  - Delayed epiphyseal ossification (femoral heads may not be seen for years); early OA.
- **SED tarda:** X-linked (TRAPPC2/SEDL), boys, late childhood, hip and back pain, platyspondyly with a "heaped-up" posterior vertebral body.
- **Kniest dysplasia** (COL2A1): **dumbbell-shaped femora**, large stiff joints, myopia and **retinal detachment**, hearing loss, cleft palate.
- **Stickler syndrome** (COL2A1, COL11A1): myopia and retinal detachment, Pierre Robin sequence, early OA.

## 5. Other named dysplasias
- **Diastrophic dysplasia** (AR, **SLC26A2** sulfate transporter, common in Finland):
  - **"Hitchhiker" thumb** (short, proximally placed, abducted first metacarpal), **cauliflower ears** (cystic swelling in infancy), cleft palate.
  - **Rigid clubfeet** (very resistant to treatment), joint contractures, **cervical kyphosis** (can cause quadriplegia: monitor and fuse), scoliosis.
- **Cleidocranial dysplasia** (AD, **RUNX2/CBFA1**, master gene for osteoblast differentiation):
  - **Absent or hypoplastic clavicles** (shoulders can be brought together in front of the chest), **delayed closure of fontanelles** and wide sutures with **wormian bones**, **supernumerary teeth** and delayed tooth eruption, **coxa vara**, wide symphysis pubis.
  - Usually needs no treatment; coxa vara with Hilgenreiner-epiphyseal angle over 60 degrees needs valgus osteotomy.
- **Metaphyseal chondrodysplasias:**

| Type | Gene / inheritance | Features |
|---|---|---|
| **Schmid** (commonest) | **COL10A1** (type X collagen), AD | Mild short stature, **coxa vara**, genu varum, waddling gait. **Looks like rickets but calcium, phosphate, ALP and vitamin D are normal** |
| **Jansen** | **PTH/PTHrP receptor** (activating), AD | Severe, **hypercalcaemia**, hypophosphataemia |
| **McKusick (cartilage-hair hypoplasia)** | **RMRP**, AR (Amish) | Fine sparse hair, **immune deficiency**, Hirschsprung disease, risk of lymphoma |
| Shwachman-Diamond | SBDS, AR | **Pancreatic insufficiency**, neutropenia |

- **Mucopolysaccharidoses** (lysosomal storage, defective glycosaminoglycan breakdown; urinary GAGs raised):

| Type | Name | Inheritance | Key features |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | **Hurler** (alpha-L-iduronidase) | AR | Coarse face, **intellectual disability**, corneal clouding, gibbus (thoracolumbar kyphosis), carpal tunnel syndrome; stem-cell transplant |
| II | **Hunter** (iduronate sulfatase) | **X-linked recessive** (the only XLR MPS) | Like Hurler, **no corneal clouding**, milder |
| **IV** | **Morquio** (galactose-6-sulfatase; keratan sulfate) | AR | **Normal intelligence**, short trunk, pectus carinatum, **odontoid hypoplasia with atlantoaxial instability** (occipitocervical fusion often needed), ligament laxity, genu valgum, corneal clouding |

  - **Radiographs (dysostosis multiplex):** oar-shaped ribs, bullet-shaped phalanges, anterior beaking of lumbar vertebrae (inferior beaking in Hurler, central in Morquio), proximally pointed metacarpals.
- **Osteopetrosis (marble bone disease):** **failure of osteoclast resorption**.
  - **Infantile malignant** (AR; TCIRG1, CLCN7): marrow failure (anaemia, hepatosplenomegaly), cranial nerve compression (blindness, deafness), early death without **haematopoietic stem cell transplant** (osteoclasts are of haematopoietic origin).
  - **Adult benign (Albers-Schonberg, AD, CLCN7):** fractures, osteomyelitis of the mandible.
  - **Carbonic anhydrase II deficiency:** with **renal tubular acidosis** and cerebral calcification.
  - **Radiographs:** dense, brittle bones, **bone-in-bone**, **Erlenmeyer flask** distal femora, **rugger-jersey spine**, sandwich vertebrae.
  - Fractures heal slowly; **drilling and fixation are difficult** (very hard bone; use cooled drills and plates rather than nails).
- **Pyknodysostosis** (AR, **cathepsin K**): dense bones, short stature, **acro-osteolysis** of terminal phalanges, open fontanelles, obtuse mandibular angle, fractures. (Toulouse-Lautrec is thought to have had it.)
- **Camurati-Engelmann** (TGF-beta 1): symmetric **diaphyseal** cortical thickening, leg pain, waddling gait.
- **Melorheostosis:** "dripping candle-wax" cortical hyperostosis along one sclerotome; pain and contractures.
- **Osteopoikilosis** (multiple small sclerotic islands near joints, asymptomatic) and **osteopathia striata** (linear striations): incidental findings.

## 6. Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI)
- About **90% are COL1A1 or COL1A2 mutations** (type I collagen, quantity or quality), usually AD; recessive forms involve collagen-processing genes (CRTAP, LEPRE1/P3H1, SERPINF1 etc.).
- **Sillence classification:**

| Type | Severity | Sclerae | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | Mild, non-deforming | **Blue** | Commonest; fractures decrease after puberty; **hearing loss** (third decade) |
| II | **Perinatal lethal** | Blue | Crumpled long bones, beaded ribs |
| **III** | **Most severe in survivors**, progressive deformity | Blue at birth, whiter with age | Very short, wheelchair-dependent, **dentinogenesis imperfecta**, triangular face |
| IV | Moderate | **Normal (white)** | Variable deformity |
| V | Moderate | Normal | **Hyperplastic callus**, **calcification of the interosseous membrane** of the forearm (limits rotation), radial head dislocation; IFITM5; normal collagen |

- **Other features:** **wormian bones** in the skull, ligament laxity, easy bruising, basilar invagination, scoliosis (common, progressive; bracing ineffective; fuse curves over about 45-50 degrees), **dentinogenesis imperfecta**, hyperthermia under anaesthesia.
- **Bisphosphonates** (cyclical IV **pamidronate or zoledronate**) increase bone density and **reduce fracture rate and pain**; they do not cure the collagen defect. **Denosumab** has been tried (rebound hypercalcaemia on stopping).
- **Surgery:** correct long-bone bowing with **multiple osteotomies and intramedullary fixation** (**Sofield-Millar "shish-kebab" osteotomies**). **Telescoping rods** that elongate with growth (**Fassier-Duval**, Bailey-Dubow, Sheffield) reduce reoperation. **Avoid plates** (stress risers, peri-plate fractures).
- **Differential: non-accidental injury.** OI is suggested by blue sclerae, wormian bones, osteopenia, dentinogenesis imperfecta, family history, and fractures in hospital.

## 7. Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)
- AD, **neurofibromin** (chromosome 17), a tumour suppressor (Ras-GTPase activating protein). Half are new mutations.
- **Diagnostic criteria (2 or more):** 6 or more **cafe-au-lait spots** (over 5 mm before puberty, over 15 mm after), 2 or more neurofibromas or one plexiform neurofibroma, **axillary or inguinal freckling**, optic glioma, 2 or more **Lisch nodules** (iris hamartomas), a distinctive osseous lesion (**sphenoid wing dysplasia or long-bone cortical thinning / tibial pseudarthrosis**), a first-degree relative with NF1.
- **Orthopaedic problems:**
  - **Dystrophic scoliosis:** **short, sharp, angular** curves (often kyphoscoliosis), **rib penciling**, vertebral scalloping, enlarged foramina, dural ectasia. **Rapid progression**; bracing fails; early **combined anterior and posterior fusion** (high pseudarthrosis rate). Non-dystrophic curves behave like idiopathic scoliosis but can "modulate" into dystrophic curves.
  - **Congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia:** **anterolateral bowing** of the tibia in infancy (about half have NF1). **Protect with a total contact orthosis to prevent fracture**; avoid osteotomy for the bow. Once a pseudarthrosis develops: excision with **intramedullary rodding and bone grafting**, **Ilizarov bone transport**, or **vascularised fibular graft**; bone morphogenetic protein and cross-union techniques. Persistent non-union may end in amputation. (Compare: **posteromedial bowing** is benign and associated with calcaneovalgus foot and leg-length discrepancy; **anteromedial bowing** goes with fibular hemimelia.)
  - **Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour** (about 10% lifetime risk; a painful, enlarging plexiform neurofibroma needs MRI and PET).
  - **Hemihypertrophy**, overgrowth (elephantiasis neuromatosa), non-ossifying fibromas.

## 8. Tumour-like dysplasias
- **Hereditary multiple exostoses (multiple osteochondromas):** AD, **EXT1 (chromosome 8) or EXT2 (chromosome 11)**.
  - Sessile and pedunculated osteochondromas pointing away from the joint; short stature, **forearm deformity** (**ulnar shortening**, radial bowing, radial head dislocation), genu valgum, ankle valgus.
  - **Malignant transformation to secondary chondrosarcoma** in about 1-5% (much higher than a solitary osteochondroma, under 1%). Warning signs: **pain or growth after skeletal maturity**, **cartilage cap over 2 cm** in adults (MRI).
- **Ollier disease** (multiple **enchondromatosis**, unilateral predominance, non-hereditary; IDH1/IDH2 mutations): limb shortening and angular deformity; chondrosarcoma risk about 25-40%.
- **Maffucci syndrome** (enchondromas + **soft-tissue haemangiomas**, phleboliths): higher malignancy risk, including **non-skeletal malignancies** (gliomas, gastrointestinal cancers).
- **Fibrous dysplasia** (**GNAS1** activating mutation, postzygotic): polyostotic forms cause the **shepherd's crook** proximal femur. **McCune-Albright syndrome:** polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, **cafe-au-lait spots with "coast of Maine" borders**, precocious puberty.
- **Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva:** **ACVR1** mutation, **short great toes (hallux valgus) at birth**, progressive heterotopic ossification along fascial planes. **Never biopsy or operate** (flare-ups).

## 9. Chromosomal and connective tissue conditions with orthopaedic features
- **Down syndrome (trisomy 21):** **atlantoaxial instability** (atlanto-dens interval over about 5 mm), ligament laxity, **hip instability (dislocation in later childhood)**, **patellofemoral instability**, flatfoot, slipped epiphysis, scoliosis.
- **Marfan syndrome** (FBN1, fibrillin-1; AD): tall, arachnodactyly (**Steinberg thumb sign**, **Walker-Murdoch wrist sign**), **upward lens dislocation**, **aortic root dilatation**, scoliosis (larger, more rigid, higher complication rates), **protrusio acetabuli**, **dural ectasia**, pectus.
- **Homocystinuria** (cystathionine beta-synthase, AR): marfanoid habitus with **downward lens dislocation**, **intellectual disability**, osteoporosis and **thrombosis** (anaesthetic risk).
- **Ehlers-Danlos syndrome:** joint hypermobility, skin hyperextensibility; vascular type (COL3A1) has arterial rupture; avoid stabilisation surgery where possible (poor results).
- **Larsen syndrome** (filamin B): multiple congenital dislocations (knees, hips, elbows), cervical kyphosis, flat face.
- **Turner syndrome:** short stature, **cubitus valgus**, short fourth metacarpal, **Madelung deformity**.

> Exam pearl: **FGFR3 = achondroplasia (interpedicular distance narrows caudally, foramen magnum stenosis). COMP = pseudoachondroplasia and MED. COL2A1 = SED congenita, Kniest, Stickler (eyes!). SLC26A2 = diastrophic (hitchhiker thumb). RUNX2 = cleidocranial. COL10A1 = Schmid. GNAS = fibrous dysplasia. EXT1/2 = HME. ACVR1 = FOP.**

> Exam pearl: Screen the **C1-C2** level before anaesthesia in **Morquio, SED, pseudoachondroplasia and Down syndrome**; watch **cervical kyphosis** in diastrophic dysplasia and Larsen syndrome.

## 1. Pathophysiology
- **Acute haematogenous osteomyelitis (AHO)** starts in the **metaphysis**: nutrient artery branches end in **sinusoidal loops beside the physis** where blood flow is slow and turbulent, the capillary endothelium has gaps, and there are few phagocytes. Minor trauma may create a haematoma that seeds bacteria.
- **Spread:** pus raises intraosseous pressure, tracks through the **Haversian and Volkmann canals** to the subperiosteal space, and lifts the loose paediatric periosteum (**subperiosteal abscess**). Cortical bone loses its blood supply (from both sides) and dies: **sequestrum**. The elevated periosteum lays down new bone: **involucrum**. Openings in the involucrum through which pus escapes: **cloacae**.
- **Age-related anatomy:**
  - **Under about 18 months:** **transphyseal vessels** cross the physis, so metaphyseal infection spreads to the **epiphysis and joint** (combined osteomyelitis and septic arthritis; physeal and epiphyseal damage).
  - **Childhood:** the physis is a barrier; infection stays metaphyseal and spreads subperiosteally (thick, loose periosteum).
  - **Adults:** periosteum firmly attached; infection spreads within the medullary canal and into the joint once the physes close.
- **Joints where the metaphysis is intra-articular** (osteomyelitis can rupture into the joint): **proximal femur (hip)**, **proximal humerus (shoulder)**, **proximal radius (elbow)**, **distal lateral tibia (ankle)**.
- **Septic arthritis destroys cartilage quickly:** bacterial toxins and **proteolytic enzymes from neutrophils** (proteoglycan loss within hours, collagen within days). The **hip is the emergency**: raised intracapsular pressure can tamponade the retinacular vessels and cause **AVN of the femoral head**.

## 2. Organisms by age and setting
| Setting | Organisms |
|---|---|
| **Neonate (under 2 months)** | **Group B streptococcus**, **Staphylococcus aureus**, Gram-negative enteric bacilli (E. coli), Candida in NICU babies |
| **6 months-4 years** | **S. aureus** and **Kingella kingae** (the commonest cause of osteoarticular infection in this age group where PCR is used) |
| **Older children** | **S. aureus** (by far commonest at all ages), group A streptococcus |
| Adolescents (sexually active) | Neisseria gonorrhoeae (septic arthritis, tenosynovitis, skin pustules) |
| **Sickle cell disease** | **Salmonella** is characteristic (bowel infarcts allow bacteraemia), S. aureus also common |
| **Puncture through a sneaker** | **Pseudomonas aeruginosa** (osteochondritis of the foot) |
| Unvaccinated child | **Haemophilus influenzae type b** (now rare) |
| Cat or dog bite | Pasteurella multocida |
| Chronic granulomatous disease | Aspergillus, Serratia, Burkholderia |
| India (endemic) | **Mycobacterium tuberculosis** in subacute cases, dactylitis, monoarthritis |

- **MRSA** (community-acquired, especially **Panton-Valentine leukocidin (PVL)-positive** strains): severe sepsis, **multifocal disease**, **deep vein thrombosis and septic pulmonary emboli**, necrotising myositis, more surgery.
- **Kingella kingae:** Gram-negative coccobacillus in the oropharynx of toddlers, often after a viral upper respiratory infection. **Mild illness, low-grade or no fever, normal or mildly raised CRP and WBC.** It grows poorly on standard media: **inoculate blood-culture bottles** with joint fluid and use **PCR**. Treat with a cephalosporin (resistant to clindamycin, glycopeptides).

## 3. Clinical features
- **AHO:** fever, malaise, **localised metaphyseal tenderness**, pseudoparalysis (refusal to use the limb), limp; swelling and erythema later.
- **Septic arthritis:** severely painful joint, **refusal to bear weight**, held in the position of maximum capsular volume (**hip: flexion, abduction and external rotation**), pain on any passive movement (log-roll), fever.
- **Neonates:** **few systemic signs**; irritability, pseudoparalysis, poor feeding; **multifocal** disease is common; high risk of joint destruction.
- **Psoas abscess, pyomyositis, discitis and sacroiliitis** can mimic septic hip: discitis in toddlers presents with refusal to walk or sit; pyomyositis (S. aureus, tropical) with a tender, woody muscle.

## 4. Investigations
- **Blood:** WBC, **ESR** (rises over days, falls slowly over weeks), **CRP** (rises within 6-8 hours, peaks at 48 hours, **normalises within about a week of effective treatment**: the best marker of response), **blood cultures** (positive in about 30-50%).
- **Kocher criteria (septic arthritis vs transient synovitis of the hip):** **non-weight-bearing**, **temperature over 38.5 C**, **ESR over 40 mm/h**, **WBC over 12,000/mm3**.

| Criteria present | Predicted probability of septic arthritis |
|---|---|
| 0 | about 0.2% |
| 1 | about 3% |
| 2 | about 40% |
| 3 | about 93% |
| 4 | about 99.6% |

  - **Caird** added **CRP over 2 mg/dL** (20 mg/L) as an independent predictor; **fever over 38.5 C is the best single predictor** in that study. Later validation studies showed lower accuracy in other populations: use the criteria as a guide, not a rule.
- **Imaging:**
  - **Plain radiographs:** soft-tissue swelling and loss of fat planes early; **bone changes (lysis, periosteal reaction) appear only after about 10-14 days** (30-50% loss of bone mineral needed). Baseline and to exclude differentials.
  - **Ultrasound:** **hip effusion** (absence of an effusion makes septic hip very unlikely), subperiosteal collections; guides aspiration.
  - **MRI** is the **investigation of choice for osteomyelitis**: marrow oedema (T1 low, T2/STIR high), subperiosteal and intraosseous abscess, physeal involvement, adjacent septic arthritis, pyomyositis. Contrast helps define abscesses.
  - Bone scan (Tc-99m) if the site is unclear or multifocal disease is suspected; can be cold early in severe infection (compromised blood flow).
- **Aspiration** (joint or subperiosteal pus) under ultrasound or fluoroscopy before antibiotics if it does not delay treatment: Gram stain, culture (plus blood-culture bottle and PCR for Kingella), cell count. **Synovial WBC over about 50,000/mm3 with over 75-90% neutrophils** suggests septic arthritis (lower counts in Kingella and early infection).

## 5. Treatment
### Antibiotics
- Start **empirical IV antibiotics immediately after cultures**: **anti-staphylococcal** cover (cefazolin or cloxacillin/flucloxacillin; **add vancomycin or clindamycin where MRSA is prevalent**; add cefotaxime/ceftriaxone in neonates and where Gram-negatives or Kingella are possible).
- **Short IV course with early oral switch** (current evidence, e.g. the Finnish trials of Peltola et al.): switch to high-dose oral antibiotics after about **2-4 days** once the child is clinically improving (afebrile, less pain) and **CRP is falling** (about 50% reduction).
- **Total duration:** **septic arthritis about 2-3 weeks**; **uncomplicated AHO about 3-4 weeks**; longer (6 weeks or more) for MRSA, complicated disease, neonates, pelvic and spinal infection, slow response.

### Surgery
- **Septic arthritis of the hip is a surgical emergency:** **arthrotomy and thorough washout** (anterior approach; some use arthroscopy) as soon as possible. Other joints (knee, ankle, elbow) may be managed by arthroscopic washout or repeated aspiration in selected cases.
- **Osteomyelitis: operate** for a **subperiosteal or intraosseous abscess** (drill the cortex, drain the pus), **no clinical improvement after 48-72 hours** of appropriate antibiotics, sequestrum, or concomitant septic arthritis.
- Immobilise briefly for comfort (splint); early mobilisation once pain allows. Watch for **pathological fracture** in extensive osteomyelitis (protect with a cast).

## 6. Complications
- **Physeal arrest** leading to limb-length discrepancy or angular deformity.
- **AVN of the femoral head** and **hip dislocation or destruction** after septic hip (the neonatal destroyed hip is **Tom Smith arthritis**; Hunka and Choi classifications of sequelae).
- **Chronic osteomyelitis**, **pathological fracture**, recurrence.
- **DVT and septic emboli** (PVL-MRSA), sepsis and multi-organ failure.
- **Joint stiffness, early arthritis**, cartilage loss.

## 7. Subacute and chronic osteomyelitis
- **Subacute osteomyelitis (Brodie abscess):** low virulence or partial treatment; insidious pain, few systemic signs, often normal markers.
  - Radiograph: well-defined metaphyseal (or epiphyseal) lucency with a **sclerotic rim**, sometimes crossing the physis.
  - **Differentials: osteoid osteoma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, chondroblastoma (epiphysis), Ewing sarcoma (diaphysis).**
  - **Roberts classification** of subacute osteomyelitis (types by location and appearance); biopsy and curettage when the diagnosis is uncertain.
- **Chronic osteomyelitis:** **sequestrum, involucrum, cloaca, sinus**.
  - **Treatment:** **sequestrectomy and debridement** to healthy bleeding bone (**paprika sign**), but **wait until the involucrum is strong enough** to support the limb (otherwise fracture or segmental loss); dead-space management (antibiotic beads or cement, bone graft later), soft-tissue cover, prolonged antibiotics guided by deep cultures.
  - Long-standing sinus: watch for **Marjolin ulcer (squamous cell carcinoma)** in adults.
  - **Cierny-Mader** staging (anatomical type I-IV and host A, B, C) is used in adults.
- **Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CRMO; chronic non-bacterial osteomyelitis):** autoinflammatory, **sterile cultures**, recurrent multifocal bone pain (**medial clavicle**, metaphyses, spine), associated **palmoplantar pustulosis, psoriasis or inflammatory bowel disease** (SAPHO in adults). Whole-body MRI; **NSAIDs** first line, then bisphosphonates or anti-TNF agents; not long-term antibiotics.

## 8. Special forms
- **Neonatal osteoarticular infection:** NICU babies with umbilical or central lines; multifocal; minimal signs; **combined osteomyelitis and septic arthritis** (transphyseal vessels); high rates of growth disturbance and hip destruction.
- **Discitis (toddlers, about 1-5 years):** the **disc is vascular in young children**. Refusal to walk or sit, back pain, abdominal pain. Mild fever, raised ESR/CRP. **MRI** shows disc space narrowing with endplate oedema. Treat with **antibiotics (anti-staphylococcal) and rest/brace**; biopsy rarely needed.
- **Pelvic osteomyelitis and sacroiliitis:** buttock, groin or abdominal pain, mimics septic hip or appendicitis; FABER test; MRI.
- **Puncture wound osteochondritis of the foot (Pseudomonas):** usually osteochondral (metatarsal heads, calcaneus); needs surgical debridement plus anti-pseudomonal antibiotics (ciprofloxacin, ceftazidime).
- **Sickle cell crisis vs osteomyelitis:** both cause bone pain, fever and raised markers. Infarction is far commoner; osteomyelitis is suggested by persistent fever, a single site, positive blood cultures, and fluid collections on ultrasound/MRI. **Salmonella cover** (e.g. ceftriaxone or ciprofloxacin) in empirical treatment. **Dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome)** in infants is infarction.
- **Gonococcal arthritis** (adolescents): migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, pustular skin lesions; ceftriaxone.
- **Lyme arthritis** (endemic regions): large-joint effusion with moderate pain and less fever; serology.
- **Osteoarticular tuberculosis in children (India):**
  - Insidious monoarthritis (hip, knee), **"spina ventosa"** (tuberculous dactylitis: expanded phalanx or metacarpal), spinal TB (see Spine notes).
  - **Phemister triad:** juxta-articular osteopenia, peripheral erosions, gradual joint space narrowing.
  - Diagnosis: histology (caseating granulomas), **GeneXpert/CBNAAT** (also detects rifampicin resistance), culture.
  - **Multidrug therapy** for about 12 months under the national programme; surgery for abscesses, debridement, deformity.

## 9. Differential diagnosis of the irritable hip in a child
| Condition | Key features |
|---|---|
| **Transient synovitis** | Commonest cause of acute hip pain (3-8 years), often after a viral illness, mild or no fever, able to bear some weight, near-normal markers; resolves in 1-2 weeks with rest and NSAIDs |
| **Septic arthritis** | Toxic, febrile, refuses weight bearing, raised markers (Kocher, CRP) |
| Perthes disease | 4-8 years, insidious limp, mild pain, normal markers, radiograph or MRI changes |
| SCFE | Adolescent, often obese, Drehmann sign |
| Osteomyelitis (proximal femur, pelvis) | Focal tenderness, MRI |
| Juvenile idiopathic arthritis | Morning stiffness, more chronic, other joints, uveitis risk |
| Malignancy (leukaemia, Ewing) | Night pain, systemic features, abnormal blood count, bone lesion |

> Exam pearl: **Metaphysis = commonest site; S. aureus = commonest organism at all ages; Kingella = 6 months-4 years (PCR, blood-culture bottles); Salmonella = sickle cell; Pseudomonas = sneaker puncture.**

> Exam pearl: **MRI is the investigation of choice for osteomyelitis; radiographs lag 10-14 days.** **CRP is the best marker to monitor response.** **Septic hip = emergency arthrotomy.**
